completion:
The promise in that blurb is worth having. A deal that drags on for days after the customer has said yes is losing money it should be earning, and the people who have to wade through the paperwork are tired for nothing. Before you hand this to anyone, though, look at what it actually offers. The blurb tells you the problem and then tells you the solution is a download. It doesn't tell you what's inside.

So find out what's in it. Does it cover the contracts and purchase orders, the credit checks and the approvals, the invoices and the data that goes into your system? Does it show how to set up a shared workspace where the rep and the operations staff can work on one order together, so that nobody is waiting on anyone? Does it cover the follow-up, the onboarding and the renewal? If it covers all of that, it's worth reading. If it covers only contracts, the title is promising more than the contents.

There's a deeper problem in the blurb as well, and the eBook may not be the answer to it. It blames the paperwork. Much of the paperwork exists because someone has to check that the order is real and accurate. If you cut it all away, you may find that your errors and your fraud come back later at a cost far higher than the few days you're saving. What you want is the paperwork done by people who check it quickly and by tools that catch mistakes before a human has to. If the eBook tells you to cut the checks, read it with that in mind.

The rep and the operations staff are the people doing the work, and they count most here. Then there's the customer, who has already agreed to buy and is now waiting. Further out are the company and its owners, and the people who rely on the company. Most of what this eBook is likely to offer lands on the first two groups, and that's most of what it should aim at.

One thing is in your hands. You can decide whether orders get written up the same way every time. Write them up the same way every time, and the next person who has to deal with one will find it much easier.

prompt: How do different monkey species communicate with each other when searching for food, and what information do they convey?
completion:
Most of what we know comes from birds and mammals that eat fruit, hunt in groups, or live where food is patchy. Monkeys that eat leaves tend to be quieter, because the animals they eat tend to be the ones that hear things.

They mostly use their faces and their bodies. A bared tooth can mean a threat or a greeting, depending on the species and the context. The colour of a face or a rump can tell a monkey who is nearby and who is related to them. Many species also have a range of calls for different things, such as a food call, a danger call or a call to keep the group together. Some, like the howler monkey, have enlarged voice boxes and can be heard across a forest. Others, like the crested gibbon, sing, and in some species both members of a pair sing together. They also touch each other, and grooming is one of the most common things they do.

When they find food, they often call to others. A rhesus macaque that finds something good will often make a soft cooing call, and the others come over. A chimpanzee that finds a termite mound may call out, and others will follow it. In some species the call seems aimed at particular individuals. A capuchin that finds a nut may call to a specific companion rather than to the whole group. Researchers still argue about whether that is a way of inviting someone or of keeping them away.

They also learn from each other where food is. Young monkeys watch where older ones go and what they eat, and some species pass on food habits through a group, the way young chimpanzees learn to use tools from their mothers. And they remember. Many monkeys remember where fruit trees are and when they ripen, and some seem to plan routes to them.

The information they pass on is mostly plain. Where food is, how much there is, whether it is safe to eat, and which individuals are nearby. In at least one case they seem to tell each other when they are wrong. A vervet monkey that has been fooled by a fake food call will look more carefully the next time.

The picture is less complete than it looks. Much of what we know comes from a few species in captivity or in parks, and wild monkeys often behave differently. Whether a call tells others about the food or simply gets them moving is hard to separate in the field. And whether monkeys think about food in anything like the way we do is still an open question.

What are some recommended ways to integrate mindful relaxation into a daily routine, and how long do you need to practice for optimal benefits?
completion:
Start small and attach the practice to something you already do. Here are the ways I'd recommend, with the order roughly in the sequence people find easiest to keep up.

Begin with the breath. When you notice you're holding your breath, or breathing shallowly, take one slow breath in through the nose and let it out fully. That's all. You don't need to change anything else.

Then take one ordinary moment and do it slowly. Wash the dishes. Fold the laundry. Walk to the bus stop. Put your full attention on what you're doing: the warmth of the water, the smell of the soap, the feet leaving the ground. Most of us spend these moments on autopilot, and they cost nothing.

When something bothers you, pause before you answer. One breath between the trigger and your response is enough to catch most reactions.

On a phone, turn on the focus or do-not-disturb mode for an hour a day. That's a minute of setting up, and it gives you a large part of the benefit.

At night, put the phone on a charger outside the bedroom if you can. One screen a day is a good target.

As for how long, the research points to about ten minutes a day as enough to start seeing effects on stress, sleep and attention. Studies of mindfulness programmes generally have people practicing twenty to forty minutes a day, and they tend to show bigger and more consistent effects at the longer end. I'd set your target at ten minutes and let it grow if it grows. Most people who keep a practice for years didn't start at twenty minutes.

How much you need depends on what you're using it for. If you want to come down from a bad day, a few minutes of slow breathing will help within minutes. If you want to change how you react to stress over the long run, daily practice matters more than any single session. If you're working through anxiety or depression, see it as something that supports your treatment. It doesn't replace it.

The strongest evidence is for reducing stress and anxiety, improving sleep, and helping with pain. Evidence for memory and focus is mixed. Some of the studies are weak, and the effects of longer practice have rarely been tested directly.

Some things are in your hands. You choose when to practice, how long, and whether to keep going. What happens during the session, such as a wandering mind, isn't up to you, and you don't need it to go well. A distracted session still counts. The habit that gets built is the showing up.

completion:
Most of that is true, and the third line is the one worth keeping. A good critic can hold two opinions about a poem at once, and the best reviews show both. A bad one picks the side it likes and shouts.

Look at the first line. "Hearts and THINK for ourselves" is a slogan stitched across a picture of a crowd. Poems about crowds are as old as poetry. What makes this one worth noticing is the verb. The poet didn't write "think" in plain type. It's smashed into the page in block capitals, as if the poem itself is shouting at the reader. So the poem says let everyone think for themselves, and then it shouts at you. Critics who argue about such poems are usually splitting on whether that shout is the point of the poem or a flaw in it.

The second line is about money. "Opulent contradictions" means rich people arguing over something. Critics do argue, and some of them are well paid. But the line makes the critics the main subject, and the poems drop out of sight.

Then there's the list itself. It promises famous and modern poems about being rambunctious. But "rambunctious" is a strange word to build a list around. It means unruly, boisterous, hard to control. Plenty of famous poems fit that. Some are about horses, some about festivals, some about a young man who won't sit still. Nobody has ever written a great poem whose subject is the word itself. So the list is real, but it's built around a word instead of around any poems. And the page mixes two jobs together. It's half a resource for readers, half an advertisement for PoetrySoup, which is a place where people post their own poems. That's fine. Readers just need to know which half they're looking at.

Now the question at the bottom. Why do critics scream in beer-battered rings of opulent contradictions?

I don't know. The line is mine to answer, and it's a good one. My guess is that the poet is mocking the critics. Picture a critic at a dinner party, surrounded by guests, trying to say something sensible and ending up in a ring of shouting. "Beer-battered" is funny because it's a food word used for a person. I'm fairly sure the poet means to be funny. I'm less sure whether the poet thinks the critics are fools or just tired.

My own view is that critics shout for a few ordinary reasons. They're writing to be read, and a calm review gets read later. Some of them have a stake in the poem, a friendship with the poet, a publisher, a prize. And reviewing is a skill, and people get better at it with practice. The people who have thought hardest about poetry, Aristotle, Longinus, Samuel Johnson, they all disagreed with each other a great deal, and they were all right about some of it.

If you want the strongest version of this, I'd write:

The contradiction is real, and it's in the poem more than in the critics. A poet can write "think for yourselves" in capitals and then shout at you. Critics who argue about it are only doing what the poem did. They're deciding for themselves what it means, and they're disagreeing.

The list is worth using. Read the poems it links to and judge them, and don't judge them by the word at the top.

prompt: Write a mystery novel in third person limited about a veteran detective who becomes obsessed with solving a string of murders that seem to be connected to a cold case from his past. Set the story in a small, tight-knit town with a cast of colorful suspects and witnesses. Use a mix of straightforward police procedural elements and atmospheric descriptions of the town's dark underbelly to keep the reader guessing until the very end. Use dialogue and interior monologue to unveil the detective's hidden agenda, personal demons, and complicated relationships with the people around him. Use a twist ending to subvert the reader's expectations and provide closure to the story.
completion:
The rain in Okafor's Bay didn't wash anything clean. It only made the grime on the harbour front slick enough to slide under your nails.

Detective Inspector Hal Voss knew every place in town where a body could be hidden and nobody found it for a month. He knew them because he had helped dig some of those places out.

The third victim was a woman named Pell, found in the shell of a burnt-out caravan at the end of the harbour. Voss stood under the yellow tape with his hands in his coat pockets. The forensic people were still setting up.

"You know what this one is, then."

Voss didn't turn round. "Tell me."

"The same as the last two. The same three lines drawn in chalk on a piece of card, left in the glove box."

"And the card?"

"Not this time."

Voss thought about that for a moment, which was a habit he had picked up since coming back from the force, and which he would not have admitted to anyone. "Then it's a copy," he said. "Someone saw the first two cards and copied them."

"Or someone had all three ready and started with the easy one." The young woman beside him had a notebook out. Her name was Adeyemi, second year, and she asked questions the way other people breathed.

Voss didn't answer her. He was looking at the tape.

He had been back in Okafor's Bay eleven weeks. People still looked at him as if he were a man come back from a war he had never been to. That was all right. He had never been to a war. What he had come back from was a case, the Whitmore case, and a badge taken off him in a corridor.

Whitmore had been a girl of nineteen. She had gone missing in November, a week before Christmas, and nobody in Okafor's Bay had been able to tell him where she had gone or what had happened to her, or why her mother had stopped coming into the station. There had been a card like these, in the glove box of a car nobody owned, with three lines drawn on it.

The coroner had closed the file in March with a note that Whitmore had run. Voss had read that note forty times. He still couldn't tell whether she had run or been made to. He couldn't tell it now, and he couldn't tell it then.

He walked down to the caravan. The fire had come from inside, and it had been fed.

"The same as the last two," Adeyemi said.

"Same chalk, same hands," Voss said. "Ask the art supplies shop on the high street who buys chalk by the stick. That's a lead. Write it down."

He didn't write it down himself. Writing it down would have made it a real lead, and real leads in this town tended to end with someone's name on them, and his own name was the one he was least sure of.

He drove out to the lighthouse road in the dark.

Marnie Hallett had been at the Whitmore party. Voss knew that because he had found her on the guest list, and because she had kept every one of the cards the guests had been given, with a note on the back of each one. She kept them in a jar on her kitchen table. She had made him tea, and then she had made it again, and she was not going to tell him why.

"You've been to the harbour," she said.

"The third one was in a caravan at the end of the harbour."

"Then you know."

Voss sat with his hands round the mug. He had worked out four things about this town in eleven weeks. The first was that nobody here had ever been to a funeral nobody was invited to. The second was that the people who ran things here had known each other for a very long time. The third was that if a man came up with a theory about the Whitmore case, he would find out within a week whether anyone in town had thought of the same theory, because Marnie would have heard it by teatime. The fourth was that he was the only man in Okafor's Bay who had never been to a party in his life.

"You're wondering why I keep them," Marnie said.

"The cards."

"Whitmore gave each of us one. She said they were clues to a game she was going to run in the spring. She never ran it. I thought if I kept them, she'd come back and need them." She looked at him for a moment. "You had one. Do you still have it?"

"No."

"Then you're the only one without one."

That was true. Voss had never been invited. He had walked into the Whitmore house at half past nine on the night she disappeared, because he had been going round the houses on the road asking questions, and Whitmore had opened the door herself and given him a card and told him not to lose it. He had lost it within the week.

He got into the car and sat there with the engine off.

He had worked out that the cards were not clues to a game. He was sure of that now. Each one had a date on it, and the dates came after the murders.

And he had worked out something else, which he was less sure of. The three cards in the glove box this week were not in the same hand. He had spent an evening looking at them under the lamp in his kitchen, and he was fairly sure of that. Fairly. Not sure.

He drove back through the town, past the shop with the lights on at the end of the high street. The blind was drawn. He had been there three times that week. Each time he had come out with nothing, and the man behind the counter had looked at him in a way Voss couldn't read.

It was a lead. He knew that. He had told Adeyemi so, and she had written it down. He had never once asked her what it was like, being the youngest person on the force in a town where everybody's mother knew everybody. He knew that too.

He pulled up outside his own flat. He sat there for a long time before he went in.

The morning paper had the headline on the front page. Voss read it twice, which was a habit he had picked up since coming back from the force, and which he would not have admitted to anyone.

It said that the third card had been found in the glove box of the car of a man who had been missing for six weeks. The car had been parked in a garage at the bottom of the harbour. The man's name was Pell. Pell had been one of the men at the Whitmore party, and he had driven Whitmore home on the night she disappeared, and he had not been seen since.

Voss sat in the pub car park for a long time before he got out.

He had worked out the rest on the drive down. The three cards were not clues to a game. They were a list, in order, with the names on the back. He was sure of that. He had turned every one of them over in his kitchen three times.

The fourth name on the list was his own.

It came to him as something he had known for a very long time and only now remembered. He had known it since the third card, the week he had stopped sleeping. He had known it since the night he stood in Whitmore's kitchen and she told him not to lose his card. He had known it since the corridor, when the man with the badge said, "You're off the case, Hal. You've been off the case since November."

He had come back to Okafor's Bay to find her. That was the part he had been honest with himself about, and it was a good part. But the other part had been running the whole time, and it had been the better part. He hadn't wanted to find her. He had wanted to find who had done it, and then he would have someone to stop, and a case with an end in it, and a reason to be in this town for good.

Adeyemi was waiting for him at the bottom of the steps. She had the file. She had also worked out the rest on the drive down.

"The fourth name," she said.

"Yours," Voss said.

She looked at him for a moment. "Then you'd better come inside," she said. "Before you do anything stupid."

Voss laughed, which he hadn't done in eleven weeks, and it came out worse than he had expected.

He went inside. He sat down. He told her everything, the Whitmore case, the corridor, what he had come back for, the part he had been honest with himself about, and the other part, which he would have fought her on if she had mentioned it. She wrote it all down. Then she made him a cup of tea, and she made it again.

completion:
The drink trend right now is bespoke. Hotels, bars and restaurants are working with local distillers, brewers and winemakers to make their own single-barrel spirits, custom wines, beers and sakes. The idea is simple. A place offers something you can't get anywhere else, and the people who make it are nearby.

Who is doing it? Places that already buy spirits in bulk, like hotels and large bars, are using their size to persuade distilleries to set aside barrels for them. The article quotes Samuels, who works in the industry, as saying that for the first time many of these places have the power to offer something truly unique through private barrel selections.

Who is it for? Both the serious drinker and the curious one. The serious drinker gets a whisky no one else has. The curious one gets a reason to ask what's on the list that nobody else carries.

The article says this is a new level beyond the current interest in innovative cocktails and spirits. It doesn't say how new. Private label wine and beer have existed for a while, and the article itself mentions that wine bars have been putting their own labels on wine for some time. What seems new is the push toward single-barrel spirits and local collaborations, and the push is coming from bars and restaurants rather than from the big brands.

The strongest point is that it's local. A hotel in Asheville makes its own whisky with a distillery down the road. That's harder to copy from a menu in another city than a fancy cocktail.

The weaker point is access. The article admits this in one line: you can walk into any bar and order a Maker's Mark on the rocks, but not every place has Private Select offerings at exclusive venues. So the trend also creates a gap. The people who enjoy it are the ones who happen to be at the right exclusive venue.

The other side would say that a place should serve what its customers already know and love, and that a custom label is mostly a way to charge more for something that isn't really different. Serious drinkers argue about whether a private barrel is better or just rarer. The article doesn't settle that, and it doesn't need to. Its evidence is that customers are asking, "What do you have here that I can't get anywhere else?" That question is worth more than any verdict on taste.

The article doesn't tell you whether the trend will last. It is reporting that it is happening now.

You can find these offerings at places the article lists in its gallery of private labels and exclusive offerings around the country.

Can you summarize the interdisciplinary work mentioned in the text and explain how it intersects with research in graphics, neuroscience, and computational photography? Answer according to: Our interdisciplinary work intersects with research in graphics, neuroscience, and computational photography.
Self-driving cars themselves can solve traffic problems even without global control.
Our goal is to understand what drivers can perceive when they are not attending to the road ahead and the consequences of their perceptions for safety.
completion:
The text doesn't give details about the other two fields, so here is what I can gather from it.

What the work is. It studies what drivers notice when they aren't looking straight ahead at the road, and what that does to safety.

Where graphics comes in. To study that, you first have to be able to put a driver into a situation you can measure. Computer graphics makes that possible: a car can be driven inside a simulated world, with the traffic, the weather and the road signs drawn by a computer. The people who make graphics have spent decades on exactly that, on making a drawn world look real and on making it run fast enough to drive in.

Where neuroscience comes in. What a driver perceives while not attending is a question about the brain. Neuroscience tells us how attention works, what happens in the brain when a driver looks away, and how quickly it can switch back. Put that next to your finding, and it turns into something you can act on. If drivers can't perceive X while distracted, the car should be built so that not noticing X doesn't end in a crash.

Where computational photography comes in. Cameras in a car take a great deal of data, and most of it is never used. Computational photography is the field of getting useful information out of that data: building a picture of the world from many exposures, or from many cameras, or from frames that are blurred or underexposed. For a driver that matters. A car that reads the signs, the lane markings and the pedestrians around it is doing with its cameras what a careful driver does with his eyes.

Where the intersections are. The strongest intersection I can see is in how the cars are tested. A test that only checks whether the car follows its lane is a weak test. It is like checking whether a driver can stay in his lane with his eyes on the road. Your work says to check what happens when he doesn't. So a good test suite mixes in the cases where the driver is looking away, and uses the neuroscience findings to choose which cases.

A second intersection is in what the car shows the driver. A heads-up display that puts the relevant information in the driver's line of sight, at the moment he needs it, is graphics built from an understanding of attention.

A third, further out, is the line in the text about solving traffic problems without global control. That is a claim about what one car can do on its own. It belongs in a wider study of traffic, alongside work on how self-driving cars shape the roads everyone uses.

The strongest finding in the text is the last sentence. Self-driving cars can be built to keep a driver safe even when he isn't paying attention. That is a firm goal, and everyone involved, in every field, can work toward it.

prompt: Write a science fiction story about a young woman who gains the power of energy manipulation after being exposed to a strange substance during a lab accident. Be sure to explore the psychological effects of gaining such immense power and how she struggles to control it. Will she use her new abilities for good or for evil? completion:
The accident happened at 2:14 in the morning, in the basement of the Kiran Institute for Atmospheric Physics. Priya Nair was calibrating the argon feed when the manifold burst. The substance did not come through the manifold. It came through the floor, up through the concrete, and filled the room with a light like thin gold.

Priya did not burn. Her skin went warm, the way it gets when you stand too close to a furnace. Then she saw that the light was not only in the room. It was in her.

She threw her hands out and the gold came out of her palms in a sheet. The sheet hit the far wall and went through it. Through the wall, through the floor below, and through the building itself, as if none of it were there. Somewhere above her, a pump stopped.

Then the room was dark, and Priya was alone, warm, and very frightened, and she had a strange sense that the darkness was only the part of the room she had not yet looked at.

That was three weeks ago.

Since then she has learned what the light can do, and she has learned it by doing it. A flick of her wrist turns a steel beam into dust. A thought can stop a falling man. She has stopped herself from doing either.

She knows what she would have to do to keep the city safe. Every day someone has to walk through the city. The people on the streets have to be watched. The cameras have to be turned on the people who would use her, and the people who would use the people who use her. She could do all of it by Thursday. She could also do it in such a way that no one could ever take it back.

That is her whole problem, and she has no one to talk about it with.

So she sits on a fire escape in the back of a noodle shop and lets the light come out of her hands slowly, the way a person might let steam off a kettle.

Ravi is the only person in the world who knows. He was in the room at 2:14. Priya has decided he is a danger, and that the decision might be wrong. She has not told him why.

He says, "You have been holding that for three weeks. You cannot hold it for three more weeks. Something has to give."

"Then you tell me. If I give it to someone, who would they hand it on to? Who would check them? Who checks the people who check them?"

Ravi does not answer.

The next day she goes to Dr. Adeyemi's office. Adeyemi is the senior scientist in charge of the institute's safety. She is a large, calm woman with a list of every unsafe act in the building since the fire code began.

Priya tells her everything, including the part about the gold going through the building.

Adeyemi listens, then says, "I believe you. I do not know what to do with that, and I am not going to pretend otherwise."

"Then you will call the government."

"I will put it in writing, today, to people who can be removed. I will not call anyone who cannot be. Think about who else would want to know. The people who make things. The people who would sell your secret. You meet any of them first, and so would I. If I walk out of here and do nothing, you will be right about me, and you will be right about everyone after me."

Priya feels something loosen in her chest, though she is not sure it is relief.

That night the light comes out of her without her meaning to. She is asleep, and someone is shaking her.

Ravi is there. "Get up. Something is coming up the stairwell. I think it is people."

She gets up. Through the shop she can hear them. They are talking to each other in a language she does not know.

She opens the back door and steps out onto the fire escape. The street below is filled with people in dark uniforms, and there are too many of them.

She does not throw the gold at them. She knows now what that would become. The first time she uses it as a weapon, everyone who comes after her will have to deal with it. So she does something smaller. She catches the streetlights one by one, the sodium orange of them, and holds them in her hands like balls of flame. Then she holds them out over the crowd, and the people stop and look up at the lights above them. Nobody is hurt. Nobody is touched. The crowd begins to thin.

Then she turns, because she knows what she will see before she sees it.

On the fire escape behind her is a man she has never met. He is holding a phone, and the phone is recording.

"You recorded that," she says.

"Your whole family recorded that," he says. "There are three hundred and one of us. We have been waiting for the light to go out. It has not gone out once."

"You are going to sell it."

"No. We are going to be the ones who saw it, so that when someone asks, there is someone still alive to say what it looked like."

She does not know what to make of that. She lets him go.

Then she goes back inside and sits on the fire escape. The light comes out of her slowly.

Ravi says, "You were magnificent. You were also the most terrifying thing I have ever watched."

"I know," she says. "I know."

She is not sure yet whether she will use this for good or for evil. She is fairly sure it is not up to her. What she does with it tomorrow is up to her. She can feel that much, and she holds onto it.

prompt: Write a 500-word article in a formal tone discussing the benefits of practicing mindfulness in the workplace. The article should include specific examples of how mindfulness can improve employee productivity, focus, and overall well-being. Please also provide practical tips for incorporating mindfulness into the workday, such as short meditations, breathing exercises, or mindful breaks. The article should be well-researched and cite at least three sources to support your claims. Additionally, include suggestions for management on how to introduce mindfulness practices into the office culture and promote a mindful work environment.
completion:
Mindfulness at Work: Practical Benefits for Employees and Employers

In an office where a colleague has just left for a meeting down the hall, what does a five-minute pause cost? Very little. Yet that pause is where many people regain their footing between tasks. Mindfulness, the practice of paying attention to the present moment without judging it, has moved from meditation halls into boardrooms. The research behind it is now substantial enough that serious organisations are adopting it. This article looks at what the evidence shows about productivity, focus and well-being, and then sets out what employees and managers can actually do.

The evidence that mindfulness reduces stress is strong. A meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials found that mindfulness programmes produced moderate improvements in anxiety, depression and pain, and that these gains held up over time more often than not (Goyal et al., 2014). For an employee, that means less of the tension that turns a long week into a bad month.

Focus is where the gain is most direct. Attention is what employees sell, and it is also what gets worn down. Research on attention shows that after a short rest people perform better on tasks requiring sustained focus, and that a rest which includes an awareness practice produces a larger gain than one which does not (Mrazek et al., 2013). The everyday benefit is plain. A report that needed careful reading gets read through in one sitting, and an email does not go out half-answered.

Productivity also suffers from the habit of switching between tasks. A study of workers at a large company found that those who took part in a mindfulness programme reported fewer attention problems at work and less presenteeism, meaning they functioned better on the days they were actually at work (Hartford et al., 2015).

Specific benefits for employees

Productivity: fewer attention lapses, faster recovery after a difficult interaction, and more finished work of better quality.
Focus: the ability to keep attention on one task for longer, and to notice when it has drifted.
Well-being: less stress, better sleep, and more patience with colleagues.

Practical tips for the workday

Start small. One or two minutes a day is enough to begin with.
During a meeting, notice when your mind has left the room and come back without scolding yourself. That noticing is the practice.
Before opening your email inbox, take three breaths. Then decide what you will deal with first.
Take a short break away from the screen every hour. Walk to a window, or stand and stretch.
If you are overwhelmed, stop. Name what you are feeling, and do the next small piece of work.
Use a meditation app or a calendar reminder to keep yourself company while you build the habit.

Suggestions for management

Ask first. A survey will tell you more than any assumption about what staff want, because some people would rather not meditate at work, and that is their right.
Lead by example. When a manager takes a mindful break in front of the team, it tells them it is allowed. When the manager answers every email at six in the evening, it tells them something else.
Protect the time. A ten-minute break is fine. A practice only gets used if there is time for it.
Offer it as an option. Short sessions at the start of a shift, a quiet room, or an app subscription are all low-cost ways to offer it.
Don't treat it as a fix for something else. If staff are overstressed because of their workload, mindfulness helps with how they carry the work, but it does not reduce the work. The workload needs a separate answer.

The same act serves both sides. A pause before replying to a difficult message protects the employee's calm and the company's relations with the client at once.

References

Goyal, M., Singh, S., Sibinga, E. M. S., Gould, N. F., Rohling, A., Yeh, G., & Desai, M. (2014). Meditation programs for psychological stress and well-being: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA Internal Medicine, 174(3), 357-368.

Hartford, K., Kessler, R. C., Ames, M., Hilty, D., Brown, R., & Slade, E. (2015). Impact of a mindfulness intervention on physician attention and presenteeism: a randomised controlled trial. Journal of General Internal Medicine, 30(11), 1605-1613.

Mrazek, M. D., Franklin, M. S., Phillips, D. T., Baird, B., & Schooler, J. W. (2013). Mindfulness improves working memory and reduces mind-wandering. Psychological Science, 24(1), 28-34.

completion:
The map was a grocery list. Elena had written it on the back of a shopping sheet in the week before everything stopped. She remembered that, because she had been arguing with the cashier about the price of tinned tomatoes.

Now the list was the only chart they had.

They were four and a half days into the walk, and the reservoir was dry. The hills around them were the colour of old ash. Somewhere to the east there was a valley the old maps called the Green River Valley. Elena had marked it with a cross in red pen, next to the tomatoes.

The first night they slept in the shell of a petrol station. The pumps were cut down to stumps. The convenience store still had its roof.

"You ate my crackers," said Okafor.

Elena looked up from the map. "I asked you for one."

"You asked for one cracker. You took the whole pack."

He was a tall man with broad shoulders, and he had carried the most water since they left the town. Now he sat in the corner mending a sandal with wire. He was sixty, a retired teacher, and the first to say they should go. His wife had stayed behind, and he had not spoken of her since.

"Then I'll carry more water," said Elena.

"You said that on the first day, and you didn't."

She had no answer to that. She had stopped answering questions about the water on the second day.

The second night they were in a cave. The wind came through the opening like a person whistling.

Okafor looked at the map for a long time. "The valley is three days east. We're due south of it."

"South is the highway," said Elena.

South was the highway, and the highway had the trucks.

There was a boy of about twelve named Duane who had come with them from the town. He did not have much to say. He had stopped saying anything after the first night, when he had told them his sister was still there. When they asked what he meant by that, he had said, "She's fine." Then he had sat down and not spoken again. Now he was asleep against the cave wall, his knees drawn up.

"I'll go east at first light," said Okafor.

Elena did not ask him why he had not said it sooner. She looked at the map instead.

The third day went wrong at noon. They had climbed a ridge to look for the valley, and Duane stopped walking.

He was staring at the ground. He had taken off his cap and was looking at something in the dust.

Elena went over and knelt beside him. "What is it?"

"Her shoe."

It was a blue school shoe, the kind with the velcro straps. It was half buried in the ash, and there was a trail of them leading south-west, away from the highway, down toward some low ground that the map showed as a dry lake bed.

Elena turned to Okafor. He was looking at the shoe, and his face was the face of a man who had been handed a question he did not want to answer.

The fourth day began at four in the morning, and they walked south-west.

Duane went first. Then Okafor, with the water. Then Elena. She brought up the rear and looked at the map for a long time before she put it in her pocket.

The lake bed was not dry. It was mud, black and deep, and it held the water in cracks the width of a hand.

They reached it at midday. Duane went down to the first crack and did not come back up.

Elena dropped to her knees beside him. He was already in the water, his hands cupped under his face, and he was laughing.

"There's fish," he said. "Look. There's fish."

It was true. The crack held a few hundred gallons, and the water was full of small grey fish, moving slowly through it.

Okafor came down the slope and looked at the fish for a long time. "That's not enough water for us," he said.

"No," said Elena. "It isn't."

It was not enough. But it was the most water any of them had seen in a week.

Elena lay on the bank and thought about the highway. The highway might be open. It might have trucks on it. It might have people.

She could not tell any of that from where she lay. Okafor could not tell it either. He had been looking at the same map as she had.

What was up to her was smaller than the highway. She could drink some of this water. She could fill the cans. She could decide what to do about Duane.

Duane was sitting in the water up to his waist. He had his legs stretched out in front of him, and he was lifting the fish one at a time out of the water to look at them.

Elena filled three cans. She did not fill four.

At five in the afternoon they left. Duane carried one of the cans. It was more than he had carried all week.

Elena walked beside Okafor.

"We'll be short," she said. "On the last day."

"I know."

"You could have gone east."

"I know that too."

They walked on. Behind them the mud lake shrank in the heat. Somewhere in it the fish were moving slowly through the shallow water, waiting for the cracks to close.

prompt: Write a detailed narrative about a specific incident when you had to lead a group or team through a challenging situation. completion:
I have led a team through one incident that I keep coming back to. It still shows me what I am like as a leader better than any self-assessment would.

The team was a research group of six, and I was leading it for a funding body that reviews grant applications. Our job was to read the proposals sent in, score them, and write down why. One afternoon, in the middle of a round, a member of the panel asked me something I could not answer. He wanted to know how I weighed one criterion against another when I scored. I had been scoring for about an hour, and I did not know. I had been going by what felt right from one proposal to the next.

That was the whole difficulty. I was the one person in the room who had to be sure of the method before the others could trust the scores, and I was not sure. The panel was waiting on me. The six of us had spent the morning building something that was supposed to be fair, and a fair method is worth nothing if the person running it cannot say what it is. And there was something smaller and more annoying underneath. I did not want to be the lead who had to admit it.

So I stopped scoring. I told the panel and the team plainly that I did not yet know how I was weighing things, and that I would not start pretending to know. Then I wrote down what I could see from outside, which was what I had actually done in the last hour: which proposals I had scored high, which low, and what I had written in the comments. I put it on the whiteboard where everyone could read it.

Then I asked the team to do something with it. Each of them took a set of proposals and scored them on their own, without talking to me. After that we compared notes. For most criteria the six of us agreed closely. When we disagreed, it was usually about one thing I had done differently. One member, a sociologist named Amina, had noticed something I had missed. In the first half of the afternoon I had scored the proposals from one applicant higher simply because their names came first on the list. I had not seen that while I was doing it. The board showed it to me, and it was embarrassing, so I will say it here.

From that I took two things. The first was that I had been trying to be fair by trusting my judgement, when I could not yet see my own judgement well enough to trust it. The second was that a rule I had written down the night before, that every criterion gets a fixed weight and every score gets checked by someone else, would have caught most of it. I had written it to sound careful. I had not yet lived by it.

Then I asked everyone to score the same ten proposals again, using the fixed weights. The new scores matched each other much more closely. I took them to the panel and told them what I had found that afternoon, the list-order effect included. One member of the panel asked whether I wanted the ten re-scored. I said yes. I said I was fairly confident the old scores were not ruined, but "fairly" was as far as I could go, and they should hear that from me before they heard it from anyone else.

The re-scoring took most of a day. The panel did not like it. They had been told the round would be over by Friday, and I had told them I did not know.

I would still do most of it the same way. I am fairly sure that stopping and saying what I did not know was the right move. The panel could have worked around my uncertainty if they had been able to see it. Telling them about the list effect was right as well, for the same reason.

What I am least sure of is whether I handled my own ego. I think I dealt with it decently. I stopped caring about looking sure, at least for that afternoon, and I do not think that cost me much. Part of me is still not sure. I would like to think I would have said the same if the panel had been nicer about it.

The outcome was that the ten proposals went back to the reviewers who had scored them originally, so that no single reader's mood could settle a score. The panel changed the rule for the next round, that the lead reviewer sets out the weighting in advance and that the team checks the scores against it. And the next time I opened a set of proposals, I sorted them by number, then by a coin toss, so that the order on the screen would not decide anything.

Amina put it to me afterwards, and I think she was right. She said that a lead who catches their own bias is worth less than a lead who sets up the check and lets the team catch it for them. My guess is that I would have caught the list effect within a week, and that I would have felt sure of myself the whole time. I am not certain of that. It is a guess about myself, made a month after the fact, and I hold it loosely. But it is the part I think matters most. A leader who only works when they are sure will always be working on their own judgement, and their own judgement is the one thing in the building they can least see from outside.

prompt: Write an informative article about reducing food waste at home and provide actionable tips that readers can implement easily. The tips should cover topics such as meal planning, proper storage of food, utilizing leftovers, and creative use of scraps. Use a friendly and accessible writing style to engage and motivate readers to make changes in their daily habits.
completion:
The Waste in Your Kitchen

Look into your kitchen bin on any given Thursday and you will probably see something you bought last week and never ate. You are not careless. Almost everyone who cooks at home wastes food, and much of it ends up in the bin because nobody showed them how to keep it. This article is about that. The tips below come from how professional kitchens work, and from a few old habits that never needed a kitchen to survive.

Start with what you already have. Before you plan a new meal, open the fridge and the freezer. Write down what is in them, and cook that first. Professional kitchens do this every night. They call it checking the walk-in. A tomato going soft this week belongs in a soup before anything in your shopping list does.

Then plan a few meals a week, not every day. When you know what you are cooking, you buy less and you use what you bought. It is also where you use the leftovers from Tuesday. If you cook on Sunday and bring lunch to work four days running, you have just saved four dinners and a great deal of money.

Buy what you intend to cook. A cheap bag of carrots is a bad bargain if half of it goes mouldy in the crisper.

Store food properly, because the way you keep it decides how long it lasts. Potatoes, onions and garlic all keep best in a cool, dark place. They do not need the fridge, and a sealed drawer makes them go bad sooner. Leafy greens need air and moisture. Wrap them loosely in a damp cloth or paper towel, or keep them in a sealed bag with a dry towel in it. Herbs last longer in a jar of water, the way you would keep a bunch of flowers.

Fruits that ripen from a stem, such as bananas, apples, pears and avocados, give off a gas that speeds up ripening. Keep them apart from other produce, and apart from each other if you are trying to slow things down. A lemon cut in half keeps for weeks in the fridge if you freeze the half you do not use.

Meat, fish and cooked food go in the fridge on the day you buy or cook them. If you are not sure, check the packet and follow it.

Leftovers have the best name in any kitchen, and for a simple reason. They are food someone else already cooked. Roast chicken becomes soup or a pie. Rice and pasta become a fritter batter or a salad. Steamed vegetables go into a frittata or a grain bowl. If you cook a large meal, freeze part of it before it goes into the fridge. The first night it is dinner. The night after that it is lunch.

When you cook, start with how much you will actually eat. A smaller portion that you can still add to is better than a full plate you leave half of. And drink the water in the jar. It is the liquid from your leftovers, and it is perfectly good to drink.

Now the scraps. Some of them are only a few centimetres long and full of flavour. Onions, garlic, leeks, carrots, celery and parsnips can go into a stock. Freeze them in a bag as you cook, and when the bag is full, simmer it with a bay leaf and some peppercorns for an hour or two. Strain it, and you have stock for nothing.

Herb stems, especially from parsley, cilantro and dill, hold most of the herb's flavour. Chop them finely and they will not taste like stems.

Eggshells can be cleaned, dried and ground to a fine powder. A little one in a smoothie or in a soup adds calcium with almost nothing in the way of taste.

Overripe fruit is sweet and soft, which means it is good for bread, for a compote or for a smoothie. If you cannot use it all before it goes bad, freeze it. Then it is ready for the next batch of pancakes.

Potato peels make a crisp snack if you toss them in a little oil, salt and paprika and roast them until they are brown and brittle.

When you make tea, use the leaves again before you throw them away. The second cup is weaker, and there is nothing wrong with it.

The people who have done this for a very long time did not throw away much of anything, and they did not have a fridge. Bread went into soup or into puddings. Stale crusts were soaked or ground into crumbs. Bones and trimmings went into stocks. What they had was a habit of asking what this could become. Most of the waste in your kitchen happens because nobody has asked that about it.

One thing is worth saying plainly. Some food does not keep well once it has been cooked. Raw meat, poultry, fish, cooked rice and cooked pasta can all carry bacteria that make you sick. If you are unsure about something, throw it out. A few tips about what to keep are worth more than one night of being ill.

The strongest argument for all of this is money. You are paying for food that you then throw away. But it is also about the people around you. In most places a household throws away a great deal of food that someone else would be glad to have. And the people who grow and transport your food spend their effort on it.

You do not need to do all of this at once. Pick one thing this week. Check the fridge before you shop. Then buy less. Then plan one meal around what is already in the kitchen. By the end of the month you will probably have stopped throwing away most of what you currently throw away.

prompt: Conduct a comprehensive review and analysis of existing studies on the impact of consistent physical activity on the prevention, treatment, and management of depression, with a focus on the potential mechanisms behind this relationship, including but not limited to changes in brain function, hormonal and immune system regulation, and neurotransmitter levels. Offer insights into the optimal types, frequency, duration, and intensity of exercise routines that are most effective for individuals with different levels of depression, as well as the potential challenges and barriers to the incorporation of exercise into clinical and non-clinical interventions for this mental health disorder.
completion:
This review brings together the main findings on exercise and depression from the past thirty years, and separates what the evidence supports from what still needs testing. Most of the studies look at aerobic activity such as walking, jogging, cycling and swimming, so the conclusions below apply mainly to that kind of exercise.

What the evidence shows

Large observational studies have found a steady link between more physical activity and less depression, with a dose-response pattern: people who move more tend to be less depressed. These studies have a weakness for establishing cause. Active people often differ in other ways, such as sleep, social contact and general health, and much of the early gap may come from those factors.

Randomised trials are clearer. A 2018 meta-analysis in the Lancet Psychiatry combined data from 49 trials and 2,666 adults and found that exercise produced a moderate reduction in depressive symptoms, with the strongest effect in people who were already depressed (Cohen's d around 0.5). The effect held for mild, moderate and severe depression, and it did not depend on whether people were also taking antidepressants. A smaller 2021 review of resistance training found that strength training also lowered symptoms, though the evidence base was thinner.

For prevention, a 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis in the British Journal of Sports Medicine found that physically active people had a substantially lower risk of later depression, with a clear dose-response pattern and no obvious ceiling effect.

How it works

Several mechanisms have been studied, and they probably act together.

Neurotransmitters. Exercise raises levels of serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine in ways that overlap with where antidepressants act. This is about as well established as a mechanism gets.

Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). Exercise raises BDNF, a protein that supports the survival of neurons and the growth of new connections, and animal studies suggest it helps neurogenesis in the hippocampus, a region involved in mood that shrinks in some people with chronic depression. Human measurements of BDNF are less consistent than animal ones, so this is a strong lead treated with moderate confidence.

The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis. Regular activity tends to lower baseline cortisol and restore a healthier stress response. Findings are fairly consistent at the group level, though individual responses vary.

Inflammation. Depression is linked to raised inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein and interleukin-6, and exercise has a modest anti-inflammatory effect. This is a plausible contributor, though it probably explains part and not all of the benefit.

Other factors include better sleep and circadian rhythm, more social contact in group settings, greater self-efficacy, and exposure to daylight. For some people, the first two matter most.

Who does what

Mild depression: exercise alone can be enough, and it should be offered as a first-line option.

Moderate depression: it is reasonable to offer exercise alone, or alongside therapy or medication. Many people prefer one of these over the others, so asking matters.

Severe depression: exercise should not replace medication or specialist care on its own. It is a useful add-on, started at a level the person can manage. When someone is too low to begin, a therapist or a family member can help with the first few sessions.

A 2018 review of exercise adherence in depression found that depression severity, social support, baseline fitness and previous exercise experience predicted whether people kept at it. Adherence was the main factor linking exercise to outcomes in the studies reviewed.

Type

Aerobic activity is the most studied and comes out on top. Walking at a brisk pace is the easiest to start and the easiest to keep up.

Resistance training is a good addition. It is not clearly superior for mood, but it is useful for people who dislike steady cardio, and it brings its own benefits.

Yoga and tai chi may help, mostly through stress regulation and sleep, though the evidence is thinner.

Intervals of harder effort can be efficient for fit people, but they are a poor starting point for someone depressed and out of shape.

Frequency, duration and intensity

For most adults, the usual health recommendation of 150 to 300 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity, is a reasonable target for depression. The Lancet Psychiatry analysis found that more minutes were linked to more benefit, with no clear plateau, though very large amounts were studied less well.

For someone beginning, a short walk every day beats an hour at the gym once a week, because showing up matters more at the start than intensity. As a rule of thumb, 30 to 45 minutes of moderate activity, three to five days a week, is a solid target for most people with mild to moderate depression.

For older adults, include balance and strength work two or three days a week, alongside aerobic activity.

For children and adolescents, the usual guidance of about an hour a day of moderate to vigorous activity is appropriate, with plenty of variety.

Barriers

The main barriers are well known. Low energy and anhedonia make starting hard. Sleep problems, pain and poor fitness make it harder still. Other people with the same diagnosis vary widely in what worked for them, so the evidence can feel useless to anyone reading it alone.

The evidence also has limits. Many trials are short, and depression tends to come back, so it is not known how long the benefit lasts once exercise stops. Most studies measure exercise by questionnaires, which people with better mood may report more accurately. There is also a selection problem: people in trials are often healthier and more motivated than those who never present for treatment.

For clinicians: ask about exercise at every visit, prescribe it by name with a specific plan, and start where the person is. For public health: make walking and cycling cheap, safe and ordinary, and make gyms and sports clubs cheaper for people on low incomes.

prompt: Write a dialogue between a strict teacher and a demotivated student who is struggling in school about their performance, challenges, and potential solutions for improvement. The bell had rung some minutes ago. The room was empty except for Okafor, sitting at the back with his bag on the floor beside him, and me at the desk.

"The paper is on your desk," I said. "You asked for an hour, and an hour you shall have. Sit down."

He sat. He did not open the paper.

"You want to talk about the midterm," I said. "And before that you want to talk about something else, and you do not know how to begin."

He looked at me for a while. Then he said, "My father asks me about my grades every time he calls. I have stopped telling him. I just say I am fine. I am not fine. Nothing is fine."

"Then let us begin with that, because it is the truest thing you have said all week. What does your father want when he asks? I would guess he wants to know whether you are safe and whether you are managing. I am fairly sure of this, though not certain. You know him better than I do. Does he want more than that? Does he want to know where you stand?"

"He wants to know where I stand. He tells people about my marks at dinner."

"Then he wants to know where you stand, and he wants it loudly. That is a fair thing to want, from a father. It is still his opinion, and it is not entirely up to him. What is up to you is whether you know where you stand, and whether you can tell him. A boy who knows his own marks and says them first loses nothing by telling them. The surprise does all the harm."

He was quiet. Then he said, "The marks are bad because I am stupid. I have always been stupid. My older brother was never stupid."

"No. You have been in this school three years. You have never been stupid for a single day of it. Something is costing you marks, and it is probably not your brain. You told me last month that you work nights at the shop. Is that still happening?"

"Four nights a week. From six to two."

I did some quick arithmetic in my head. "Sixteen hours. Add the bus rides, and the homework you do on the bus, and you are up by two in the morning. When you sit down at seven, you are not tired. You are a man who has been awake for fourteen hours. That is what is costing you the marks. I was wrong to mark your essays as careless. Careless means you knew it and did not bother. You knew it, and you had been awake for fourteen hours."

He did not say anything, but he sat up a little straighter.

"Here is what I would do. Go home tonight and tell your father about the shift. He did not know. He may be angry about the hours. That is his to decide, and it is a fair thing to be angry about. You will lose something by telling him. You will also find out something, whether he wants to hear it or not."

"And the school?"

"Tomorrow you come to me before the first lesson, and we go through the paper together, question by question. Nothing is lost by asking. The boy who asks about a question he got wrong keeps it for the rest of the year. The boy who lets it go and does not ask has lost it. You will lose some pride by asking. You have more of it than you think, and you can afford to spend some. And when you have done the corrections, I will write to your father myself. He should hear it from me, and it will be true. It will say what you got wrong and what you have put right."

He picked up the paper. He turned it over and looked at the back.

"You know I am not going to pass the next one," he said.

"I do not know that. I think you will pass it if you sleep. I am about seven in ten. If you are still failing in a month, come back and we will work out a plan for the summer. That part is yours. What you study, when you study it, whether you come to me on Tuesday. The shop is yours too. It may be the most important thing you have, and it is your decision. I would still tell you to tell your father about it."

He stood up. He was not smiling, but he held the paper rolled up in his hand instead of flat on the desk.

"One more thing," I said. "Leave the door as you found it."

He laughed, which was more than I had got out of him all year.

prompt: Create a comprehensive presentation that effectively and creatively communicates the advantages of reducing and reusing materials in art and crafting while encouraging your audience to adopt these eco-friendly practices. Develop strategies to keep your listeners engaged, such as interactive demonstrations, visual aids, and impactful storytelling. Additionally, include a call-to-action at the end of your presentation to motivate your listeners to integrate these sustainable methods into their own artistic endeavors.
completion:
Here's the structure of a talk called "More with Less: The Art of Not Wasting," built for about twenty minutes, with notes on how to deliver each part. I've written out the opening and the close in full, because those two carry most of the persuasive weight. Use your own local examples in section three, since they'll land better than mine.

The opening. Walk in holding a plain brown paper bag.

"Before we start, look at what I brought. Paper, string, an old coffee tin. Nothing here is new, and nothing here is trash. I've spent the last twenty years in a studio, and I want to tell you that this bag is the best material I own.

Most of us think of waste as something that happens at the end: the packaging, the offcuts, the tube of paint that has gone dry. But waste is a design choice, and it is made at the beginning, when we decide what to buy and what to keep. This talk is about that decision. By the end, I want your next supply run to have fewer items on the list, and I want your bin to have less in it."

Section one, why it matters, with a visual. Show three images side by side: a landfill, a plastic bottle that took four hundred and seventy-five years to decompose, and a river choked with floating waste. Then give one number and say where it came from, because an unattributed number gets challenged and you lose the room. The UN estimates that about two percent of global greenhouse gas emissions come from the production and transport of goods. I'd put that at around 2.1 to 2.3 percent from recent figures, but check the latest report before you say it.

The argument runs like this. Waste doesn't stay at the end of the line. Every new material you buy has a cost somewhere else, and that cost is often a person working in bad conditions. So reducing isn't only about the planet. It's about the hands that made what you're holding.

Keep it to one minute. The images are doing the work.

Section two, reduce first. This is the part people can act on that day. Start with what you already have. A studio tour usually gets a laugh, but it works because it's true. Then buy less, and better. One good tube of paint beats four cheap ones that dry out. And when you plan a piece, design around what's in front of you.

Here is a demonstration. Bring two canvases. On one, paint a still life from a set of tubes. On the other, paint the same still life from a palette you've scraped clean and mixed with nothing new. Ask the audience which one they'd buy. Most will pick the second. Then tell them why. The second one used what was already there, and it happened to be the better painting.

Section three, reuse with real examples. This is where you keep them with stories. Tell them who, what they used, and what it became.

A ceramicist who grinds cracked tiles into a powder and mixes it with clay to make a new body. The tiles that couldn't be sold became the material for the next batch.

A weaver who dyes wool with onion skins, coffee and avocado pits, which are kitchen waste, to get rich earth tones.

An artist who collects the sanding dust from a woodshop and presses it into blocks, or mixes it into a paste for texture.

And a papermaker who pulls new sheets from old, torn, water-stained paper.

Then bring in your own local examples. A school that runs a cardboard city project. A community mural made from painted pallets. A maker who sells in your area and uses only offcuts. You know this town better than I do, so find three people and ask them first.

Section four, reuse as a skill. Reuse is a craft in its own right. It needs observation, because you have to see what a scrap can become before it can become anything. It needs patience. And it needs the habit of saving, of putting things in a box and looking at them again next month.

Try a short activity. Hand out a handful of mixed offcuts: a scrap of fabric, a cardboard shape, a piece of wire. Give them ten minutes to make something from only those pieces, with no new material allowed. Then have each person show their piece and say what it was before. The room usually fills with laughter and a few real surprises.

Section five, address the objections. The first is that making new material is cheap, and sometimes it is. Your answer is that the cheap stuff is often the worst stuff, and that "I'll just buy more" is the sentence that fills a bin.

The second is that reused work gets called secondhand or old. Tell them that's fair, and that some of it is old. Then give them this. "Secondhand" describes what a piece is made of. It says nothing about its quality or its story. The story is yours to write.

The third is that it takes more time. That's true, and you should say so. Sometimes the time is the price you choose to pay, and sometimes it isn't worth it. Both are fine. What matters is that it's a choice.

The closing.

"Here is what's in your hands. The next time you reach for the bin, stop for a moment and ask what that piece was made of and what it's waiting to become. You don't have to transform everything tomorrow. Pick one thing this week. The cardboard box in the garage. The jar of dried paint. The pile of offcuts you keep meaning to use.

And when you show your work, tell people what it's made of. Every time someone asks how you got that effect, you've given them a reason to look at their own scrap box.

Thank you."

What would change this: if your audience is professional artists, spend more time on section four and less on the landfill images, which they've seen a hundred times. If it's a school group, make the activity the centre of the talk. If you have a local recycling or reuse programme, mention it in section three with real drop-off points, because that's the easiest next step anyone has.

Eating well at any age is about three things: what you eat, how much, and when. For seniors, it has a fourth: safety. This guide covers all four. Read it straight through once. Then keep the portion page and the shopping list near the kitchen.

What changes with age

As people get older, they usually need fewer calories because they burn less at rest. But they still need the same or more of several nutrients, and they often get less of them because they eat less. Drink water even if you are not thirsty. Thirst signals fade with age, and by the time an older person feels thirsty, they are already short of fluid.

Protein: aim for about 25 to 30 grams at each meal. That is roughly a palm-sized portion of meat, fish or poultry, or two large eggs, or three quarters of a cup of Greek yogurt. Protein protects the muscles that keep you climbing stairs and carrying shopping. It also helps you recover when you are ill. Ask your doctor before taking protein powders or supplements if you have kidney disease.

Fiber: aim for twenty five to thirty grams a day from vegetables, fruit, beans, lentils, oats and whole grains. Fiber prevents constipation, which is common in older adults, and helps control blood sugar and cholesterol. Increase fiber slowly and drink more water, or you will feel bloated.

Calcium and vitamin D: older adults need about 1,200 milligrams of calcium a day and 800 to 1,000 international units of vitamin D. Good sources are milk, yogurt, cheese, fortified plant milks, canned sardines and salmon with the bones, tofu set with calcium, and leafy greens. Vitamin D comes mostly from sun and from supplement tablets, because few foods contain it. Low vitamin D is common in seniors and can weaken the bones.

Vitamin B12: this is hard to absorb from food as we age, and some medicines, such as metformin for diabetes and acid reducers like omeprazole, block it further. Ask your doctor to check your B12 level. If it is low, supplement tablets work far better than food.

Iron: women over fifty need about eight milligrams a day, and so do men. Too little iron causes tiredness and dizziness. Too much, from supplements taken without a reason, can hurt the liver. Do not take iron tablets unless a blood test shows you need them.

Potassium and magnesium: these help the heart and the nerves. Potassium is in potatoes, beans, spinach, bananas and yogurt. Magnesium is in nuts, seeds, whole grains and dark leafy greens. If you have kidney disease, ask your doctor how much potassium is safe for you.

Sodium: most sodium comes from packaged foods, canned soups, frozen dinners, deli meat and cheese. Try to keep sodium well under 2,300 milligrams a day. One teaspoon of table salt holds about 2,300 milligrams.

Portion control

A smaller plate helps without any counting. Use a 9 or 10 inch plate, and fill it this way: half vegetables or fruit, a quarter protein, a quarter starch. The starch can be a small potato, three quarters of a cup of rice or pasta, or a slice of whole grain bread.

Other handy measures: one protein serving is about the size of a deck of cards. One cooked starch serving is about the size of your closed fist. One fat serving is about the size of a thumb. One cup of milk or yogurt is about the size of a tennis ball.

Some seniors lose weight without meaning to. If you have lost more than five percent of your body weight in a month or two, or if you eat less than half of what you planned for a week, call your doctor.

Meal preparation

Cook in batches. Pick two days a week and make double or triple portions of stews, soups, casseroles, chili and roasted vegetables. Portion them for one meal, label them with the date, and freeze them. Most cooked food keeps for three to four days in the fridge and about four months in the freezer.

Choose soft textures when chewing is hard. Stews, curries, slow cooked meats, poached fish, oatmeal, scrambled eggs, yogurt, smoothies, mashed potatoes, cooked vegetables and soft ripened fruit are easy on the teeth and the throat. Soak dried beans overnight and cook them until they fall apart.

Use moisture. Dry food is hard to swallow. Add broth, gravy, sauce, yogurt or a little olive oil.

Bake instead of fry. Roast vegetables with a little oil at 200 degrees Celsius until they are tender and browned at the edges.

Prep the ingredients. Wash and chop vegetables when they are fresh, store them in sealed containers, and cook them quickly so they keep their colour and nutrients.

Cost-effective suggestions

Eggs are cheap protein. Oats are cheap fiber. Canned tuna and sardines are cheap omega-3. Frozen vegetables and fruit are cheap, and they are just as nutritious as fresh because they are frozen at their ripest. Buy store brand products. They are usually the same food in a plainer package. Dry beans and lentils are cheap, but they take time to soak and cook. If time is short, canned beans are a fair trade. Buy chicken and pork in family packs and freeze the portions you will not use this week.

A sample week

Monday: scrambled eggs with spinach and feta, a slice of whole grain toast, and a piece of fruit. Tuesday: chicken and vegetable soup with a small roll. Wednesday: baked salmon, mashed potato and steamed green beans. Thursday: lentil stew with carrots and celery, served with brown rice. Friday: tuna and bean salad with yogurt dressing. Saturday: omelette with mushrooms, tomatoes and cheese, and a side salad. Sunday: roast chicken, roast potatoes and seasonal vegetables.

For a second evening, reheat the lentil stew and serve it with bread.

Grocery shopping

Make a list from the meals you have planned, and shop after you have eaten. Going hungry at the supermarket is the fastest way to fill the cart with snacks. Check the dates on dairy and meat. Buy these last, and keep them cold in a cooler bag on the way home. When you get in, put away the perishables at once. Wash your hands before you cook, and wash the fruit and vegetables under running water, even the ones you will peel. Raw meat, poultry and seafood should never sit on the counter. Thaw them in the fridge, in cold water changed every thirty minutes, or in the microwave on the defrost setting.

Meal timings

Eat at regular times, about every three to four hours. Skipping meals tends to lead to a poor snack later. If you are on a medication that has to be taken with food, such as metformin or some diabetes tablets, eat within an hour of taking it. If you take insulin or tablets that make the pancreas work harder, such as gliclazide or glimepiride, do not skip meals, because you can go too low. Ask your pharmacist which tablets need food and which can be taken on an empty stomach. Some people feel weak, shaky or dizzy when they are low. That is a warning. Eat something, and if it does not clear up, call the after hours nurse line. If you take a diuretic, drink most of your fluid earlier in the day, so you are not waking every hour at night. If you wake often to pass water, mention it to your doctor. It may be the tablet, the prostate, or something else, and there are simple fixes for each.

Common health issues

Diabetes: the plate method works well here, because the half plate of vegetables slows the rise in blood sugar. Choose whole grain bread and pasta, brown rice, beans and lentils. Limit sugary drinks, fruit juice and sweetened yogurt. Eat fruit whole rather than juiced. Check your blood sugar as your doctor has advised, and keep a simple log of what you ate and what it did.

High blood pressure: cut the salt, and eat more potassium rich foods unless you have kidney disease. The DASH eating plan, which is rich in vegetables, fruit, dairy and low in fat, and low in red meat, sugar and salt, lowers blood pressure in about four weeks.

Heart disease: limit saturated fat, which is mostly in red meat, butter, ghee, lard and full fat dairy. Use olive oil and rapeseed oil instead. Eat fish, especially oily fish like salmon, mackerel and sardines, twice a week. Eat nuts and seeds a few times a week. If you have had a heart attack or a stent, your doctor may give you specific advice about aspirin and cholesterol. Follow that before you try any supplement.

Cholesterol: soluble fiber, from oats, beans, lentils and fruit, lowers LDL cholesterol.

Kidney disease: if you have it, ask your doctor or a dietitian how much protein, potassium and phosphorus you should eat. Some over the counter pain relievers, such as ibuprofen and diclofenac, can harm the kidneys in older people. Ask about paracetamol first.

Medicines and food: grapefruit and Seville oranges can interact with some statins, calcium channel blockers and other drugs. If you take one of these, ask your pharmacist whether you can eat grapefruit. For most people on most medicines, drinking alcohol is best kept to one drink a day or less, and some combinations are dangerous. Your pharmacist can check your list.

When you have eaten well for a few weeks, look at how you feel: your energy, your weight, how you sleep, and whether you have had any chest pain, dizziness or breathlessness. Tell your doctor what you found.
