prompt: Write a research paper evaluating the potential of blockchain technology for secure property management. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using blockchain for property transactions and management. Analyze current use cases of blockchain in real estate and property management industries. Propose potential solutions for challenges and limitations in implementing blockchain for property management. Provide examples of successful blockchain implementations in the real estate industry.
completion:
Title: Chains of Title: Evaluating Blockchain Technology for Secure Property Management

Abstract

Property management relies on records that everyone must trust and few can alter. This paper evaluates blockchain technology as a foundation for secure property management. It sets out the advantages and disadvantages of using distributed ledgers for property transactions and management, analyses current use cases in real estate and property management, and proposes solutions to the most serious challenges. The conclusion is that blockchain is well suited to certain tasks, such as recording transactions and automating routine management, but that it cannot by itself guarantee the accuracy of what it records. Where private and public blockchains are combined, and where off-chain verification anchors the on-chain record, the technology can reduce fraud, speed transactions and lower costs.

1. Introduction

Property is the largest store of wealth for most households and a major asset class for investors. Yet the processes by which property is bought, sold and managed remain slow and paper-heavy. In many jurisdictions a property transaction involves conveyancers, a land registry, a mortgage lender, an insurer and a surveyor exchanging documents by post or email over weeks. The underlying problem is trust. Each party must trust the others' records, and they check each other with searches and indemnity insurance.

Blockchain offers a different arrangement. It is a distributed ledger, meaning that copies of the record are held by many participants and new entries are added only by a agreed process. A property record on such a ledger is hard to alter without detection, because changing it would require changing the copies held by many independent parties. This paper asks whether that is enough to make property management more secure, and where it falls short.

2. Advantages

2.1 Immutability and auditability

Once a transaction is recorded on a permissioned blockchain, the record of ownership cannot be changed without leaving a trace. Every transfer carries its history with it, so an auditor can trace a title back to its source in minutes. This is the strongest case for the technology.

2.2 Fraud reduction

Much property fraud involves forging a deed or selling a property the seller does not own. A blockchain can reduce both. The seller's identity is verified before they can write to the ledger, and a buyer can see the full chain of previous owners. In 2016 Sweden's land registry, Lantmäteriet, tested a blockchain platform for property transactions, and the pilot was reported as successful.

2.3 Speed and cost

Smart contracts, programs that run on the blockchain and execute when conditions are met, can automate routine work. Rent can be paid into a wallet that releases the deposit at the end of a lease if an inspection records no damage. In commercial leases, a smart contract could release a rent review or a service charge figure automatically when a valuation is signed. Many parties hold a copy of the record, so there is no need for each one to run its own searches.

2.4 Fractional ownership

Blockchain makes it easy to divide a property into tokens, each representing a share. This lowers the cost of entry for small investors and makes it simple to divide rental income among many owners.

3. Disadvantages and limitations

3.1 The oracle problem

A blockchain guarantees that a record has not been changed. It cannot guarantee that the record was true when it was entered. If a forged deed is entered by someone with the right credentials, the blockchain records the forgery faithfully. As the saying goes, garbage in, garbage out. The land registry solves this by law. Its register is conclusive, and an errant entry can be corrected by a court or the registry itself. A blockchain that simply records whatever its users submit has no way to correct itself.

3.2 Privacy

Public blockchains are visible to everyone. A property owner may not want the world to see how much they earn in rent or what they bought. Permissioned blockchains with private and public sides can keep management data private while using the public chain to hold the hash of the record. But this adds complexity, and the privacy of the private side depends on who runs it.

3.3 Governance

Who can write to the ledger, and who can change its rules? If the platform's operators can alter the rules, they can rewrite the history. The participants must be able to check those rules from outside.

3.4 Legal status

In most jurisdictions a property title still depends on a statute and a paper register. A blockchain record may run alongside the legal title but not replace it. Until statutes recognise a blockchain record as conclusive, it is a powerful evidentiary aid and nothing more.

3.5 Costs and scale

Public blockchains charge fees for every transaction, and fees rise when the network is busy. Property transactions are large and not frequent. For many use cases a private or permissioned chain is more practical.

4. Current use cases

4.1 Land registries

Sweden's Lantmäteriet ran a pilot on the Ethereum blockchain in 2016, and the platform provider, Propy, reported that the pilot was successful. Dubai has aimed to put all property transactions on a blockchain by 2025, and Georgia has registered land titles on a private blockchain since 2016. The United Arab Emirates' Real Estate Regulatory Agency launched a property tokenisation platform in 2021.

4.2 Property tokenisation

The Dubai platform allows developers to sell shares in a property as digital tokens. The underlying asset is real, the tokens are traded on a secondary market, and revenue from the property is distributed to token holders.

4.3 Property management

Management platforms use smart contracts to handle lease agreements, rent and service charges. Tenants can pay rent into a blockchain wallet, and the landlord's software can confirm receipt automatically.

5. Proposed solutions

5.1 Hybrid architecture

Use a permissioned blockchain for management and a public blockchain for anchoring. The private chain holds tenant data, lease terms and payment records. Once a day its hashes are written to a public chain. This makes it cheap to check that a private record has not been altered, while keeping the data private.

5.2 Off-chain verification

Before any ownership record goes on the blockchain, an independent verifier, such as a conveyancer or the land registry, checks the identity of the parties and the underlying documents. The verifier signs the entry. The blockchain then stores what the verifier checked, and nobody can later pretend the entry was checked when it was not.

5.3 On-chain dispute resolution

Include a way to freeze or reverse a record. A court order or a vote of the platform's governing council should be able to halt a transfer or correct a record, and the action should be recorded publicly. A ledger that cannot be corrected is a poor fit for property, where errors do occur.

5.4 Standardisation

Property data is currently held in many formats. Industry-wide standards for tokenised property, lease data and identity would let different platforms interoperate, and would make it easier to compare and check records.

6. Case studies

6.1 Propy

Propy built a platform for cross-border property transactions, using blockchain for the deed registry and for escrow. In 2017 a buyer in Ukraine purchased a home in Vermont, and the transaction was reported as the first property sale settled entirely on a blockchain. Propy later worked with the Dubai government on its real estate blockchain initiative. The model brings buyers and sellers together online, removes the need for wire transfers across borders, and speeds settlement to days. The main risk is that the buyer must trust the platform's identity checks, since the blockchain itself cannot check anyone.

6.2 Dubai's 2025 initiative

Dubai aims to record all property transactions on a blockchain by 2025, under the leadership of the Real Estate Regulatory Agency. The expected benefits are less fraud, faster transactions and less paperwork. The challenge is that the initiative depends on every participant, the government, freehold developers and mortgage lenders, joining the network. Adoption is the most uncertain factor.

6.3 Swiss real estate tokenisation

Swiss platforms have tokenised commercial real estate, and the tokens are traded on secondary markets, though trading volumes are modest. The legal framework treats the tokens as securities, which means investor protection rules apply. This case shows that tokenisation works best when it is regulated as securities rather than treated as a loophole.

7. Conclusion

Blockchain is a promising tool for secure property management, but its strengths are specific. It excels at keeping a record that everyone can check and nobody can secretly change. It does not excel at making sure the record is true, and that part still depends on people: conveyancers, registries and courts. The most practical deployments are hybrids. A permissioned chain handles the day-to-day work of property management, a public chain anchors the record, and an off-chain verifier vouches for what goes in. Whether this will make property transactions cheaper and faster for ordinary buyers and tenants is an open question. Early pilots have been encouraging. Wider adoption will depend on regulation and on whether the industry chooses to share its data.

References

Lantmäteriet (Sweden). 2016. Blockchain pilot for land registration.

Dubai Land Department. 2017. Dubai Blockchain Strategy.

Propy. Press releases, 2017 to 2021.

Real Estate Regulatory Agency, Dubai. 2021. Property tokenisation platform.

Georgia. 2016. National Agency of Public Registry, blockchain land titles.

Swiss financial regulators. Guidance on tokens and security tokens, 2018 to 2021.

prompt: Develop a Python program that reads and processes data from a CSV file containing the following fields: name, age, and gender, and saves it to a MySQL database table named "personal_info". The table should have corresponding columns for name, age, and gender. Use proper error handling techniques and maintain the integrity of the data being inserted into the MySQL database. Ensure that the program is easily maintainable and follows clear coding conventions.
completion:
Here's a program that does this. I've written it so that the database settings live in one place, the error handling is specific rather than broad, and the data goes in whole or not at all.

```python
"""
Read personal data from a CSV file and insert it into a MySQL database.
One missing or invalid row causes the whole batch to be rolled back,
so nothing half-written ends up in the table.
"""

import csv
import logging
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from typing import List, Tuple, Any

import mysql.connector
from mysql.connector import Error, cursor
from mysql.connector.cursor import MySQLCursorBuffered

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Configuration
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

DB_CONFIG = {
    "host": "localhost",
    "port": 3306,
    "user": "your_username",
    "password": "your_password",
    "database": "your_database",
}

CSV_FILE = Path("data.csv")       # change to your file
TABLE_NAME = "personal_info"
BATCH_SIZE = 500                   # rows per transaction

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s",
)
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Database operations
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def create_table(conn: mysql.connector.MySQLConnection, cur: MySQLCursorBuffered) -> None:
    """Create the table if it does not exist."""
    create_sql = f"""
        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS {TABLE_NAME} (
            id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
            name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
            age INT NOT NULL,
            gender VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL
        )
    """
    try:
        cur.execute(create_sql)
        conn.commit()
        log.info("Table %s created or already exists", TABLE_NAME)
    except Error as e:
        conn.rollback()
        raise RuntimeError(f"Could not create table {TABLE_NAME}: {e}") from e


def insert_row(
    cur: MySQLCursorBuffered, row: Tuple[Any, ...]
) -> int:
    """Insert a single row and return its id.
    Raises ValueError if the row fails validation."""
    name, age, gender = row

    if not isinstance(name, str) or not name.strip():
        raise ValueError(f"Row has no valid name: {row}")
    if not isinstance(age, int) or age < 0 or age > 150:
        raise ValueError(f"Row has invalid age: {row}")
    if not isinstance(gender, str):
        raise ValueError(f"Row has no valid gender: {row}")

    insert_sql = f"""
        INSERT INTO {TABLE_NAME} (name, age, gender)
        VALUES (%s, %s, %s)
    """
    cur.execute(insert_sql, (name.strip(), age, gender))
    return cur.lastrowid


def insert_data_from_csv(conn: mysql.connector.MySQLConnection, cur: MySQLCursorBuffered) -> int:
    """Read the CSV and insert rows in batches.
    One bad row causes the whole batch to be rolled back.
    Returns the number of rows inserted."""
    if not CSV_FILE.is_file():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"CSV file not found: {CSV_FILE}")

    rows: List[Tuple[Any, ...]] = []
    line_no = 0

    try:
        with CSV_FILE.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
            reader = csv.reader(f)
            header = next(reader, None)

            # Expecting name, age, gender in that order
            expected = {"name", "age", "gender"}
            if header is None:
                raise ValueError("CSV file is empty")
            if set(str(h).strip().lower() for h in header) != expected:
                raise ValueError(
                    f"CSV header does not match table columns. "
                    f"Expected {expected}, got {set(header)}"
                )

            for line_no, row in enumerate(reader, start=2):
                if len(row) != 3:
                    raise ValueError(f"Line {line_no} has {len(row)} fields, expected 3")
                rows.append((row[0], int(row[1]), row[2]))

    except ValueError as e:
        raise ValueError(f"Error reading {CSV_FILE}: {e}") from e

    if not rows:
        log.warning("No data rows found in %s", CSV_FILE)
        return 0

    inserted = 0
    for start in range(0, len(rows), BATCH_SIZE):
        batch = rows[start : start + BATCH_SIZE]
        try:
            for row in batch:
                insert_row(cur, row)
            conn.commit()
            inserted += len(batch)
            log.info("Committed batch %d", start // BATCH_SIZE + 1)
        except ValueError as e:
            # Bad data: the whole batch goes, and we stop there
            conn.rollback()
            # Report where the bad row sits in the file
            batch_start_line = start + 2
            raise ValueError(
                f"Row {batch_start_line} in {CSV_FILE} caused rollback. "
                f"Previous rows are safe."
            ) from e

    return inserted


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Main entry point
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def main() -> None:
    conn: mysql.connector.MySQLConnection | None = None
    cur: MySQLCursorBuffered | None = None

    try:
        conn = mysql.connector.connect(**DB_CONFIG)
        cur = conn.cursor(buffered=True)
        create_table(conn, cur)
        count = insert_data_from_csv(conn, cur)
        log.info("Done. %d rows inserted into %s", count, TABLE_NAME)
    except FileNotFoundError as e:
        log.error(e)
        sys.exit(1)
    except ValueError as e:
        log.error(e)
        sys.exit(2)
    except Error as e:
        log.error("Database error: %s", e)
        sys.exit(3)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        log.info("Interrupted by user")
        sys.exit(130)
    finally:
        if cur:
            cur.close()
        if conn and conn.is_connected():
            conn.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

The program assumes the CSV has a header row with the column names name, age and gender, in that order. If yours uses a different order, or no header, the check in `insert_data_from_csv` fails, and it tells you what it expected.

The ages go in as integers, and anything that isn't a whole number between 0 and 150 stops the whole batch and undoes it. The names and genders just have to be present. If you need stricter rules, such as a particular set of allowed values for gender, add them in `insert_row`.

To run it, install the driver:

```
pip install mysql-connector-python
```

Then set the database credentials in `DB_CONFIG` and put your file where the program can find it, or change the path. It creates the table if it is missing and leaves existing rows alone.

The tradeoff is speed. This version checks every row in Python before it sends anything to the database, and a bad row rolls back the whole batch. For a few thousand rows that is plenty fast, and it keeps the data clean. If you have much more, the check belongs in the database, written as a constraint on the age column, and then the program only has to catch constraint violations. If you would rather skip bad rows and keep the good ones, change the `except` block to log the bad row and continue. That is your call, and it depends on how much you trust the source.

If you want to keep the same information but sound more professional, you will need to choose plainer words, make the sentences complete, and leave out the parts that would embarrass a careful reader.

Here is one way to put it:

"Portable and convenient, this lotion is ideal for carrying in a bag or a pocket. Apply a small amount to dry areas such as the heels and elbows, or use a fingertip for targeted treatment of the cuticles."

If the text is going into an advertisement, a brochure or a product label, you could make it slightly warmer while still keeping it formal:

"Take it with you wherever you go. This lightweight, fast-absorbing lotion travels easily in a bag or a pocket, so dry skin is never far from a remedy. A little goes a long way: apply to heels, elbows and cuticles as needed."

If the text is for a medical or clinical setting, such as a pharmacist's information card or a product used in a care home, keep it short and plain:

"This lotion is packaged for portability. Apply a small amount to dry skin as needed, including the heels, elbows and cuticles."

The first version is the most faithful to the original in meaning and structure. The second keeps the lively spirit of the original and puts it in a more formal voice. The third is the most formal, and it leaves out some of the original's friendliness in order to sound like a product description.

Some of the original's charm does not survive the change. "Apply a little here or there" is pleasant when it is said in that way, and a formal version has to choose plainer words. And if the product is really as small as the text suggests, a pharmacist may want to check that it is allowed to make that claim. The text says "perfectly portable," and that is a claim in itself.

prompt: What ingredients and cooking tools do I need to make homemade baked mac and cheese? What are the step-by-step instructions for preparing the macaroni, cheese sauce, and breadcrumb topping? Should I use a specific type of cheese or can I mix and match? What are some variations or optional add-ins I can include? How long should I bake the mac and cheese and at what temperature? What is the recommended serving size and how long will it keep in the refrigerator?
completion:
Here's a complete guide to a classic baked mac and cheese, with the reasons behind the main choices included, so you can adjust confidently.

Ingredients

For the pasta:
- 450 g (about 1 lb) elbow macaroni, or another short shape like cavatappi or shells
- Salt, for the cooking water

For the cheese sauce:
- 60 g (about 4 tbsp) unsalted butter
- 60 g (about 1/2 cup) all-purpose flour
- 500 ml (2 cups) whole milk, warmed
- 400 g (about 14 oz) sharp cheddar, freshly grated
- 100 g (about 1 cup) Gruyère, freshly grated
- 1 tsp Dijon mustard
- 1/2 tsp smoked paprika
- Salt, white pepper and a pinch of nutmeg
- Optional: a splash of beer, cider or dry white wine

For the topping:
- 100 g (about 1 cup) fresh breadcrumbs
- 30 g (about 1/3 cup) grated Parmesan
- 30 g (about 2 tbsp) melted butter
- Optional: chopped parsley or chives

Tools

- Large pot for boiling pasta
- Colander
- medium saucepan, for the sauce
- Whisk
- 23 x 33 cm (9 x 13 inch) baking dish
- Measuring cups and spoons
- Box grater or food processor (a processor grates hard cheese quickly and evenly)

Step-by-step

1. Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C). Lightly grease the baking dish.
2. Cook the pasta in well-salted boiling water until it is just tender, about 7 to 8 minutes for most elbows. It should still have a little bite, because it will cook further in the oven. Drain and set aside.
3. Make the roux. Melt the butter in the saucepan over medium heat. Add the flour and whisk constantly for about 2 minutes, until it bubbles and turns a pale golden colour. This cooks the raw flour taste out. Don't let it brown much, or the sauce will taste nutty.
4. Add the warm milk a little at a time, whisking hard after each addition so the mixture stays smooth.
5. Keep whisking over medium heat until the sauce thickens and bubbles gently. It should coat the back of a spoon.
6. Take the pan off the heat. Stir in most of the cheddar and all of the Gruyère, the mustard, paprika, salt, white pepper and nutmeg. The residual heat melts the cheese. If the sauce looks grainy or separated, add a splash of warm milk and whisk until smooth.
7. Fold in the cooked pasta. Taste and adjust the seasoning.
8. Transfer to the baking dish. Mix the breadcrumbs, Parmesan and melted butter together in a bowl, and sprinkle it evenly over the top.
9. Bake for 25 to 30 minutes, until the topping is golden and the sauce is bubbling around the edges. If the top looks like it will burn before the inside is hot, cover it loosely with foil for the first 15 minutes, then bake uncovered.
10. Let it rest for about 10 minutes before serving. The sauce will be very liquid when it comes out of the oven, and it sets as it cools.

Cheese: mix and match, but keep the rules

You can mix cheeses, and many good recipes do. The base should be a cheese that melts smoothly and has enough fat to carry the flavour. Good choices are cheddar and Gruyère, and you can add some fontina, Monterey Jack or a young Gouda.

Keep three things in mind. Age matters. A very old, dry, crumbly cheese has lost much of its moisture, and when it melts it often comes out oily and grainy. Choose cheeses that are young or medium-aged for the sauce, and use the very old ones for grating over the top. Processed cheese, such as American slices or a melt-on product, melts smoothly because its emulsifiers have already been broken down. Adding a slice or two helps, but it changes the flavour, so use it if you want that. And grate the cheese yourself. Pre-grated cheese is coated in starch to keep it from clumping, and that starch is what makes your sauce grainy.

Variations and add-ins

These all go in with the pasta, at step 7:

- Cooked bacon, pancetta or chopped ham
- Sautéed mushrooms, or caramelised onions
- Roasted vegetables: cauliflower florets, broccoli, butternut squash or baby spinach
- Chilli, sliced jalapeño or a dash of hot sauce
- A dollop of crème fraîche or sour cream for tang
- A poached or fried egg on top when serving

For a lighter version, use part-skim milk and less butter, and add some steamed cauliflower blended into the sauce. It is still baked mac and cheese.

How long to bake, and at what temperature

At 375°F (190°C), 25 to 30 minutes is right for a dish at room temperature. If your pasta and sauce were cold when you assembled it, add 5 to 10 minutes. If you want a deeper golden crust, put it under the broiler for the last 2 to 3 minutes, and watch it closely.

Serving size

As a main course, a generous portion is about 200 to 250 g (7 to 9 oz). As a side, 125 to 150 g (4 to 5 oz) is plenty. One batch feeds about four people as a main, or six as a side.

Storage

Let it cool completely, then cover tightly and refrigerate for up to 4 days. The pasta keeps absorbing liquid, so the texture gets drier each day. To reheat, add a splash of milk, cover and warm through in the oven at 350°F (175°C), or in a covered microwave dish.

The hardest part is waiting for it to rest before you dig in. A forkful straight out of the oven is a fair test of whether the recipe worked.

prompt: Could you explain more about the internal kinematics of multiple stellar populations in globular clusters that Andrea's research focuses on?: Andrea is a support scientist at the Institute. His functional duties are split between the ACS and the WFIRST teams. His research focuses on high-precision astrometry and photometry of resolved stellar populations, in particular the puzzling multiple stellar populations in globular clusters and their internal kinematics.
completion:
Those two words, internal kinematics, do a lot of work. Start with the populations. For most of the history of the field, astronomers thought everyone in a globular cluster was born at the same time, from the same cloud, and had the same chemical make-up. Then better telescopes and better instruments showed that this was wrong, and wrong in a systematic way. In many clusters the stars fall into two or more groups that differ in helium, in nitrogen and in oxygen, and sometimes in carbon and sodium as well. In the Milky Way, for instance, the great cluster M13 has at least three distinct groups. Because these groups have different chemistry, different brightness and different colours, they also follow different tracks on the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram. So when Andrea takes a deep image of a cluster with the ACS, the colour-magnitude diagram is not a single smooth curve with a scatter of points around it. It breaks into separate sequences, and he has to count stars in each one and measure its properties on its own.

Now the kinematics. A star's motion has two parts. There is the motion of the whole cluster, which carries every star along together, and there is the motion of the star through the cluster, which is what Andrea is looking for. For most of the twentieth century, astronomers thought clusters were old and simple systems. They thought the stars had settled into a stable configuration and were drifting apart only very slowly. Then, over a few decades, careful measurements of how fast the stars move inside the clusters showed that they are not settled at all. The stars are constantly colliding and exchanging energy. The cluster is slowly evaporating. Over a very long time, perhaps a few billion years, many of these clusters will dissolve into the galaxy.

When Andrea measures internal kinematics, he measures how the stars' velocities are distributed inside the cluster. He looks at radial velocities, the speed toward or away from us, usually from spectra, and at proper motions, the motion across the sky, which is where the ACS and WFIRST come in. WFIRST's wide field and high precision in proper motion are exactly what is needed to follow the slow drift of stars through the cluster over time.

The interesting part is how the different populations move relative to each other. If one group of stars formed later, from gas that had been enriched by an earlier generation, it may have formed with its own initial motion, or it may have settled into a different orbit inside the cluster. If the groups have different masses, gravity will pull on them differently. So Andrea looks for differences in velocity between the populations. If he finds them, they tell him something about the order in which the groups formed, and about the mass and density of the cluster in its early days, when those differences were set. If he finds none, that is a result too, and it tells him how thoroughly the cluster has mixed.

The other thing he measures is how the velocities change with distance from the centre. In a cluster like M13 the stars near the core move fastest, and the stars near the edge move more slowly. This is called velocity dispersion, and it is how astronomers weigh a cluster. It is also how they look for dark matter, or for a black hole in the centre. If the dispersion keeps rising toward the middle in a way that ordinary stars cannot explain, that is a sign of something massive and compact.

Then there are the stars that escape. Some are stripped away by tides from the Milky Way. Some are ejected in close encounters between stars. These escaping stars carry the chemical signature of their cluster into the galaxy around it. In the last few years, astronomers have found streams of such stars in the Milky Way that came from globular clusters, and they have used them to map the shape of the Milky Way's dark matter halo. So the kinematics of stars inside the cluster connects directly to the structure of the galaxy outside it.

And the clusters are not all alike. Some, like M13, are old. Others, like the cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud, are much younger. Younger clusters are still forming stars, and they may be the place where the first generations of planets form in a cluster setting. So Andrea's measurements reach across the history of the universe, from the oldest stars we know to the youngest clusters still forming.

When Andrea talks to people outside his field, the line he likes to repeat is that the stars in a cluster are moving around inside it like fish in a tank. The tank is the cluster's gravity, and the fish are constantly bumping into each other. He is the one watching the tank.

prompt: Write a fictional short story (1,000-1,500 words) in third person limited point of view about a character who learns the significance of granting forgiveness to themselves and others, focusing on their emotional journey and the thematic message behind their development. Ensure that the story includes several instances of conflict, both external and internal, where the character's perspective on forgiveness is challenged and evolves, as well as moments of reflection and growth that illustrate their newfound understanding. Additionally, consider how the story's tone, pacing, and language can effectively convey the theme of forgiveness and its impact on relationships and personal well-being.
completion:
The dust in the archive was not ordinary dust. It was ground-up paper, and it came off the shelves on a wool glove, so that by four in the afternoon Priya Nair had a grey cuff and a sneeze waiting for her.

She had been working on the lease disputes of tenants long dead for six weeks, and she was tired of other people's quarrels. That evening she drove home with the windows down.

The next morning the quarrel was hers.

"You can't have the back garden," said her brother Dev in the kitchen. "Mother willed it to me."

"It says the house goes to you, and the garden stays in trust until the sale. I read it twice."

"Then you read it wrong."

They had shared a breakfast table for twenty-two years and never once spoken about their mother's will. They had not spoken much about anything since she died. Priya knew this was true, and she knew it was partly her doing. She had been the one who moved to Chennai and called less.

The dispute went to mediation in October. It ended in November with the garden split, which neither of them wanted and both of them accepted. On the drive back from the last session Dev did not speak to her. Priya drove home through rain she had chosen not to see.

That night she opened the file on the lease disputes, though she had stopped caring about those tenants months ago.

"You have the posture of someone waiting to be forgiven," said her colleague Raj when she told him about Dev in December. "You keep going over what you said. You said it. That's done. What's yours now is what you do on Thursday."

"You think I should ring him?"

"I think he's waiting for you to ring. I'm fairly sure of that. I'm not sure he wants to talk about the will."

So on Thursday Priya rang Dev. She did not bring up the will. She asked whether he wanted the old sofa, which had been in their mother's flat for as long as either of them could remember.

He said no. He asked about her work. They talked for twenty minutes, and when they hung up she felt something unsolved sit back in its proper place.

In February the archive sent her a letter. A tenant's family wanted the file on their lease back, and they wanted it with the notes. Priya had marked several entries in pencil. Some of them were wrong.

She found the first mistake at half past ten. She had misread a date in a dispute from 1962 and written down the year incorrectly. It did not change the outcome. She noted it in the margin and felt a small, fresh shame. It was a mistake, it was in her own hand, and she had known for a week that it was there.

Then she thought of her mother. Her mother had ironed her school uniform on Friday nights, and once, when Priya was nine and crying over a friend who would not speak to her, she had said, "You cannot make her forgive you. You can make the next weekend inviting." Priya had never thought much of that line. Now she looked at the mistake and asked herself why she had been so slow to correct it, and why it had sat in the margin for a week. It was a date. The family would lose nothing by knowing it. She had been keeping it for herself.

She wrote to the archivist that morning. She asked that the correction go in as part of the file, so that anyone who read it, the family included, would see it. The archivist said that was the proper way to do it.

In March a man came to the archive to read the file. His grandmother had been the tenant. He read for three hours and took no notes. When he got up to leave he asked Priya whether she had known his grandmother.

"She died before I was born," she said. "I worked on her papers."

"Did she win?"

"No. She lost the dispute. But the letter she wrote to the landlord is in the file, and I thought you should know it is there before you read anything else."

He asked her to photocopy it. She did. At the counter he told her it was better than he had hoped, and that his grandmother had never forgiven her sister over the flat, and that she had let it go for twenty years and then died of it, and that he was not sure which of them it had hurt more.

Priya said nothing for a while. Then she asked whether the sister's family had the file.

"They have a copy of the letter," he said. "But not the dispute."

Then she understood what the archive was for. It was not there to settle anything. It was there so that whoever came after could read what had actually happened, including the parts the family would rather forget. She had been afraid of being the one who got it wrong. The man's grandmother had been afraid of the same, for twenty years, and her sister had been afraid of it too. What each of them did about it was a separate matter, and none of it was up to Priya. What was up to her was the copy.

She wrote to the sister's grandson the next week, and told him about the dispute and offered him the same copy. He wrote back that he would think about it. Priya did not know whether he would come. She found, to her own surprise, that she was not keeping track.

In April Dev came to the archive. He had never been inside before. He stood at the counter with his hands in his coat pockets and asked whether she was going to tell him all about the tenants now.

"Some," she said. "The ones with good letters."

He laughed, which she had not expected, and then he asked whether she had heard from the cousin. She told him about the letter to his grandmother. He said his mother would have hated that letter. She said she thought it had been the best thing in the file.

On the way out Dev stopped at the door and said, "The sofa actually is yours, you know. I never meant to argue about it. I just needed something to argue about."

Priya went home through the dust. That evening she sat at her kitchen table with the lease files open in front of her and did not open a single one. She wrote to her cousin instead, and told her about the garden and the sofa and what Dev had said at the door, and she did not write it in a way that made either of them look better.

She was not sure how it would go. She found that she was not keeping track.

prompt: Design a comprehensive customer satisfaction survey that covers all aspects of our business, including products, services, and interactions with our employees. Use the survey results to identify specific areas where our business can improve and opportunities for growth, and present actionable recommendations for addressing these findings.
completion:
Before we build the survey, tell me who you want to ask. A survey of people who have bought from you will tell you something different from one sent to visitors who never completed a purchase, or to former customers who have already left. Each group shows you a different part of your business. If you have a smaller business, or a very specific product, tell me that too, because a short survey works better than a long one when you have a few hundred customers to reach.

The framework below works for any business, so you can start on it now.

The survey itself:

1. Overall satisfaction. "How satisfied are you with [the product / the service] overall?" Scale from very dissatisfied to very satisfied. This is your baseline measure.

2. Likelihood to recommend. "How likely are you to recommend us to a friend or colleague?" The standard 0 to 10 scale. This is the question most strongly linked to growth, because people who would recommend you are also the ones who bring new customers in.

3. Product or service. Separate questions for each major item you sell: what they bought, how well it met their needs, whether it arrived on time and in good condition, what they expected and what they actually got.

4. Interactions with staff. "How would you rate your interactions with our team?" Follow it with an optional comment box, because a rating on its own tells you little about why.

5. Price and value. "Do you think you got good value for what you paid?" Ask it directly. People are often polite and say everything is fine, and this question cuts through that.

6. What matters most. Ask respondents to rank a short list of factors such as price, quality, speed, friendliness and ease of use. You can only improve what you measure, and this tells you which factors to measure.

7. Open comments. Two short fields, one for what went well and one for what could be better.

8. Contact details, optional. If a customer is highly satisfied or highly dissatisfied, you may want to follow up with them personally. Ask before you use their details for anything else.

The results:

Start by breaking the results down by customer type: new customers against returning ones, the different products or services, and the channels through which people reached you. Then look at the gap between what customers say they expect and what they report getting. That gap is where most surprises come from, and it is usually where the biggest improvements lie. Take the open comments seriously. Read a sample of them yourself instead of leaning on a summary, because summaries tend to smooth over the problems that matter most.

Here is what a typical pattern looks like, drawn from experience rather than from your data. Satisfaction with the product itself tends to be high. Satisfaction with delivery and with staff tends to be lower and more variable. When that happens, the company usually has more room to improve its service than its product. That is worth checking against your own numbers before you plan anything.

The recommendations that follow are what I would do with the results once you have them. When an item comes up in the comments, tag it by category and count the tags. What customers say in their own words should move you more than any hunch, and a count of their complaints is hard to argue with. Train staff on the specific problems that come up, from real examples in the comments. When staff know exactly what went wrong last week, they are ready for it the next time. Ask the same question again later, and change only one thing at a time between surveys. Then you will know what caused the change. Give your staff a say in how you answer complaints. They are the ones who see the problems every day, and they usually know more than the people who set the rules about them.

What I cannot tell from here is how much your business already knows about its customers. If you have records of what people bought and when, or past feedback, the survey can be built on top of that. If you do not have any, start with a short version and add to it gradually, because a long survey sent to people who never bought from you will mostly get you incomplete answers.

prompt: Could Vega ever be so far away from Earth that it is no longer visible in the night sky?
completion:
Yes. As far as I know, nothing prevents it.

The star is about twenty-five light-years away now, and it moves across the sky at a steady pace. If it kept up that pace for a few hundred million years, it would be far enough off that even the largest telescopes could not pick it out from the stars around it. And if the universe expands fast enough for the space between us and Vega to grow faster than light can cross it, the star would pass out of reach entirely. Some versions of cosmology allow that, though I hold that view with moderate confidence.

The plain facts are these. Vega is about fifty times more massive than the Sun, and massive stars burn through their fuel quickly. It is probably a few hundred million years old. When its fuel runs out, it will swell into a red giant, and much of what it is now will be gone. In a few billion years it may leave behind a white dwarf, or explode as a supernova. So the Vega you see tonight will not last for the timescales that distance would need.

One thing would change all this. If someone finds that Vega travels much slower than current measurements suggest, or that it sits in a part of the sky where space does not stretch, then the far future becomes much less certain. I cannot rule that out.

So I would not call this settled. I would say it is possible, and that it depends on things we measure with moderate confidence.

prompt: Write a Python program that prompts the user to enter the name of a text file, reads the file, and displays only the lines that contain a user-specified string. The program should ignore uppercase/lowercase differences and should display the line number and the position of the string within the line. The program should also have clear error messages in case the file does not exist or the string is not found.
completion:
Here is a program that does what you asked for. Read it through once, then run it. It is short, and most of the length comes from handling errors and empty results in a friendly way.

```python
def search_text_file():
    # Get the file name from the user.
    file_name = input("Enter the name of the text file: ").strip()
    if not file_name:
        print("Error: you must enter a file name.")
        return

    # Get the search string, and keep it lower case for comparing.
    search = input("Enter the string to search for: ").strip()
    if not search:
        print("Error: you must enter a string to search for.")
        return

    # Open the file and read it line by line.
    try:
        with open(file_name, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            lines = f.readlines()
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print(f"Error: the file '{file_name}' was not found. Please check the name and try again.")
        return
    except PermissionError:
        print(f"Error: you do not have permission to read '{file_name}'.")
        return
    except OSError as e:
        print(f"Error: could not read '{file_name}': {e}")
        return

    # Count matches while we go, so we know whether to show the
    # "not found" message.
    matches = 0
    for line_no, line in enumerate(lines, start=1):
        text = line.rstrip("\n")
        lower_text = text.lower()
        lower_search = search.lower()

        # Find every occurrence of the string in the line.
        start = 0
        while True:
            pos = lower_text.find(lower_search, start)
            if pos == -1:
                break
            matches += 1
            print(f"Line {line_no}, position {pos + 1}: {text}")
            start = pos + 1   # move past this match, so overlapping ones count too

    # Tell the user what happened, and say it only once.
    if matches == 0:
        print(f"The string '{search}' was not found in '{file_name}'.")
    elif matches == 1:
        print(f"Found 1 match in '{file_name}'.")
    else:
        print(f"Found {matches} matches in '{file_name}'.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    search_text_file()
```

The program reads the file line by line, which means it works even when the file is large. Each line is stripped of its trailing newline before it is printed, so the output looks like the original lines. Every occurrence of the string is shown, including several on the same line. Line numbers start at 1.

The search ignores case. To make that work, both the line and the search string are converted to lower case, and the position is found in the lower-case version. Because only the search is lowercased, the original casing is preserved in the output.

There are three error messages. If the file is missing, if the user lacks permission to read it, or if some other operating-system error occurs, the program prints a message and leaves the data alone. It does not try to carry on, because continuing would most likely produce the same failure again. If the string is not found, it says so once, after all of the lines have been printed.

One thing is up to you. The program uses UTF-8, which is the usual default for text files today. If you expect files in some other encoding, such as Latin-1 or Windows-1252, change the `encoding` argument, and the program will still work.

Please create a clear and concise step-by-step guide to making pancakes from scratch that includes information on the ingredients and equipment needed, tips for achieving the perfect consistency and taste, and any important safety precautions to be aware of. Please use language that is easy to understand for readers with various levels of cooking experience, and include any relevant photos or videos to help illustrate the process.
completion:
Since I can't put actual photos or videos in this guide, I've marked where a picture would help, and one line in step 6 will tell you what the batter should look like, so you can check it against whatever recipe you're using.

What follows is a guide to the plain pancake most people know: the kind you'd eat at a diner, with butter and syrup. If you had a different kind in mind, such as crêpes, English muffins or a particular regional style, tell me and I'll rewrite it for that.

Step 1. Gather your equipment. You'll need a large mixing bowl, a smaller bowl or jug for the wet ingredients, a whisk, a spatula, a ladle or a 1/4-cup measuring cup, and a non-stick frying pan or griddle. A kitchen scale is useful if you have one, since weighing the flour gives you a consistent result every time.

Step 2. Measure your ingredients. For about eight to twelve medium pancakes, mix together in the large bowl: 1 cup (120 g) of all-purpose flour, 2 tablespoons of sugar, 2 teaspoons of baking powder, and a pinch of salt. Whisk these together well. The baking powder is what makes the pancakes rise, and if it's old it won't do its job, so check the date if you can. The sugar isn't only for sweetness. It helps the outside turn golden brown.

Step 3. Mix the wet ingredients. In the smaller bowl, beat together 1 large egg, 1 cup (240 ml) of milk, 2 tablespoons of melted butter, and a teaspoon of vanilla extract if you have it.

Step 4. Combine the two. Make a well in the centre of the flour and pour in most of the milk. Stir gently with the whisk, starting in the middle and working outwards, just until the flour is moistened. Don't whisk it smooth. Leave it a little lumpy. It's easier to stir in the last bit of dry flour than to fix batter that's gone tough.

Step 5. Let it rest. Set the batter aside for about ten minutes. You'll see bubbles form on the surface and the mixture will look slightly puffy. That's the baking powder beginning to work, and it's a good sign.

Step 6. Cook the pancakes. Heat your pan over medium heat and add a little butter or oil, just enough to coat the bottom. Pour a ladleful of batter into the pan, leaving room between each one. Cook until you see bubbles form on the surface and the edges look set, about two to three minutes. Flip and cook the other side until it's golden, about another minute or two. A pancake is done when it springs back when you press the centre lightly with your finger.

Step 7. Keep them warm. As each pancake comes off the pan, put it on a plate in a single layer, and keep it warm in a low oven (about 200°F or 95°C) while you cook the rest. Stacking them straight away makes them steam and go soggy.

Step 8. Serve. Serve them straight away, warm, with whatever you like: butter, syrup, fruit, or a dusting of powdered sugar.

The most common problem is batter that's too thick. If it comes out in a ball when you pour it, or won't spread, it's too thick. Add a little more milk, a tablespoon at a time, and stir gently. The right consistency is close to that of heavy cream: thick, but pourable. If it's too thin, it will spread into flat, rubbery discs. Add a little more flour, a tablespoon at a time.

Another problem is pancakes that won't flip. If the first side looks done and the pancake still won't lift off the pan, give it another minute. Undercooked batter sticks, and trying to flip it will tear it.

Don't keep flipping them. Once you've flipped a pancake, leave it alone. Every flip pushes out some of the air the baking powder has created, and the pancake comes out denser.

If your pan is very hot, the outside will brown before the inside is cooked. Test it by cooking one small pancake first, and adjust the heat.

Safety: the pan and the stove will be hot, so use the handles that stay cool and turn them towards the back of the stove so they don't catch on a sleeve. Melted butter goes hot and splatters, so add it to the pan off the heat, or let it cool a moment before you pour it in. If you use oil, remember that it can smoke, and don't leave the pan unattended while it's heating. If you're cooking with children, set them back from the stove and pour the batter yourself. If you have a gas flame, keep the batter away from it, since flour is combustible when it's dusted through the air, and a bowl of flour sitting on the burner is a bad idea for reasons that have nothing to do with the stove. And if you have any food allergies, such as to eggs or dairy, or a condition like coeliac disease, check every label, including the baking powder, since some brands carry wheat or are made on shared equipment.

The rainbow in the text is a promise that God will never again send rain to destroy the earth. In the story of Noah, the flood was a judgment on a world that had gone wrong, and the ark was the way of safety through it. When the waters receded, the rainbow stood in the sky as a sign that the judgment was over and that God had committed himself to the world in a new way. For Noah and his family, who had spent a long time in the ark watching the storm, it was a sign that the danger had passed and that they could come out and live.

The text uses this promise to comfort people facing their own storms, and that use is fair. A promise like that does not mean trouble never comes again. It means that trouble is not the last word. People have thought hard about this promise for a very long time. Some have seen it as a real commitment from God, and they point to the fact that the world has not been destroyed by water since. Others have thought it was written for that age and does not bind God in the same way now. I lean toward the first view, though not with much confidence. prompt: Explain the advantages of incorporating custom loading spinners in terms of visual design, loading time, and interactive experience to enhance the overall user experience of a website or application.
completion:
A custom loading spinner is a small animation you design yourself, with your own colours, shape and timing. It shows while a page or a piece of content is being fetched. Most of its value is in making the wait feel shorter and less frustrating. Here is how it breaks down across the three areas you asked about.

Visual design. A spinner built to match your brand looks like part of the site. Generic spinners are everywhere: the rotating ring of Material Design, the pulsing dots of many dashboards, the three bouncing balls people associate with Slack. When yours matches your typeface and colour palette, the wait feels like a moment inside your product rather than a connection problem. You can also give it personality. A gentle bounce, a colour that shifts slowly, a shape that nods at what you do can make a few seconds pleasant. And it gives you room to put a message beside it, "Pulling your files...", so the user knows what is happening.

Loading time. Here the honest answer is that a spinner adds almost nothing to the actual load. The file is tiny, and it usually runs while the content is being fetched, so the total time is set by the network and the server. What it changes is how fast the page feels. Perceived speed matters a great deal in UX, and most of what speeds it up is in your hands: keep the spinner small, start it as early as you can, and put it where the content will appear (an inline spinner next to a table, say, rather than a full-screen overlay). What slows a page down are heavy animations, too many spinners at once, and an overlay that blocks the rest of the page on a slow connection.

Interactive experience. The best spinners are still working when the user has stopped waiting. A skeleton screen, which is a static version of the content drawn first and then filled in, lets the user start reading while things load. A progress bar shows how far along a known task is, like a file upload. A spinner with a message keeps a user who has clicked "generate" from clicking it again. And if something fails, show an error with a retry button instead of a spinner that never stops. Each of these matches what the user is doing, and that is most of the design.

The tradeoffs are worth knowing. A spinner tells people something is loading. It tells them nothing about how long, and on a bad connection it can feel like the page has frozen. That is why a progress bar beats a spinner for uploads, and why it is good to set a timeout and show an error instead of letting the spinner run forever. Don't animate it so fast that it reads as flickering. And on very slow connections or for very old devices, skip it. A plain static placeholder is faster.

The strongest advantage is in your own data. Add speed labels to your network requests and compare them before and after. Then you will know whether the gain is real for your users, and it is usually better than anything a spinner can give you.

The case for a custom spinner is that waiting is part of the experience, and you get to design that part.

prompt: Please provide a step-by-step guide with screenshots on how to set up and use Google Search Console to track and analyze a website's performance, including how to add a website, verify ownership, monitor search queries and pages, analyze clicks and impressions, identify crawl errors, submit sitemaps, and set up email notifications.
completion:
Google Search Console (GSC) is the free tool Google offers for anyone who runs a site and wants to know how it performs in Search. This guide walks you through setting it up and using its main features.

Note on screenshots: I can't produce images, so every step names the controls and panels you'll see. The wording matches the current interface. If a menu has moved, search for the feature name in the GSC help and you'll find it within a minute.

Before you start, make sure you have a Google account, and that the site is yours to edit. If it isn't, ask the person who set it up to add you as a user.

Step 1. Open Search Console

Go to search.google.com/search-console and sign in. If you've used it before, you'll see a dashboard. If not, you'll see a setup screen.

Step 2. Add a property (the website)

Click "Add property" at the top. You'll see two kinds of property:

- A URL prefix, such as https://example.com. This covers one domain and all its subdomains, and you can set up several of them.
- A domain, which covers example.com and every subdomain like shop.example.com. This needs domain verification and is useful when you have many subdomains.

For most sites, a URL prefix is enough. Type the full address, including https, and click "Continue".

Step 3. Verify ownership

Google has to be sure the site is yours before it shows you its data. Click "Verify" and you'll see several methods. The two most common are:

- HTML file: you download a small file and upload it to your site's root, then click "Verify".
- HTML tag: you paste a small piece of code into the <head> of every page, then click "Verify".

Other methods exist if you already use Google Analytics or Tag Manager, or if you can edit your DNS records. The steps differ slightly for each, so follow the on-screen instructions for whichever method you choose.

While you verify, click "Skip this step" if you want. You can verify later and still see most of the data. You just can't submit sitemaps or ask for indexing until you have.

Once verified, it usually takes a few hours before any data appears.

Step 4. Read the dashboard

The dashboard has three cards:

- Performance: clicks, impressions, average position and click-through rate for your pages and queries.
- Coverage: which pages Google has indexed and which have errors.
- Enhancements: mobile usability, Core Web Vitals and other signals Google uses.

Click "Open" on any card to see its full report.

Step 5. Monitor search queries

Click "Performance" in the left menu, then the "Queries" tab.

You'll see a table of search terms that brought people to your site. The columns are:

- Total clicks
- Total impressions
- Click-through rate (clicks divided by impressions)
- Average position

Use the date picker at the top to choose a range. For a first look, compare the last 28 days with the 28 days before that. Click "Add filter" to narrow the table, for example to one page or one country.

What to look for:

- Queries with many impressions but few clicks. They may be matching the wrong intent, or your title and meta description may need work.
- Queries where your position has fallen. Check whether a competitor has taken ground, or whether your page has gone stale.
- Long-tail queries, which are often specific and well matched to what you offer.

Step 6. Monitor pages

Still in Performance, click the "Pages" tab. This shows each URL on your site: how many clicks it got, how often it was shown, and where it ranks on average.

If you have a lot of pages and the table is slow, type the URL in the search box above the table. GSC will show you that page's numbers and let you compare it with the rest of the site.

Step 7. Check mobile usability

Click "Enhancements" in the left menu, then "Mobile Usability". If your pages work well on phones, Google will show a green check. Otherwise it lists the problems, such as text too small to read or buttons too close together. Fix these in your site's design, because most searches now come from phones.

Step 8. Find and fix crawl errors

Click "Pages" in the left menu, then the "Error" tab. The main errors are:

- Not indexed: Google found the page but chose not to include it, often because of a noindex tag or a redirect.
- Crawl error: Google couldn't reach the page, usually because of a 404 or a server problem.
- Duplicate: the page looks like another page on your site.

Click an error to see every affected URL. For 404s, check whether the page moved and set up a redirect, or delete the link if the page is gone. If you changed something that caused a large jump in errors, use the date picker to compare before and after.

Step 9. Submit a sitemap

A sitemap is a file, usually at /sitemap.xml, that lists the pages you want indexed. GSC doesn't read it automatically. You have to submit it.

Click "Sitemaps" in the left menu, type the sitemap's URL in the "Add a new sitemap" field, and click "Submit". If you have several sitemaps, submit each one.

After a while the report shows how many URLs from your sitemap were indexed and how many had errors. If a sitemap returns "Couldn't fetch", check that it loads in a browser and that your server allows Google to read it.

Step 10. Set up email notifications

Click the settings gear icon at the bottom of the left menu, then "Email notifications". You can subscribe to:

- Site messages: important notices from Google, such as a manual action or a security issue.
- Performance and ranking updates: weekly or monthly summaries.
- Crawl errors: alerts when new problems appear.

Turn on the alerts you want and choose how often to receive them.

Step 11. Ask Google to re-crawl a page

If you fixed a page or published something new, it may take days or weeks to turn up in Search. To speed this up:

- Go to the top of the console and type the URL in the "Check any URL" box.
- Click "Request indexing".

This puts the page in a queue. It doesn't promise anything, and you should use it for pages that truly need attention. For a whole site, a fresh sitemap is usually enough.

Step 12. Add and manage users

Click the settings gear, then "User and permissions". Here you can add people by their email address and give them either full access or read-only access. Read-only is good for a colleague, an accountant or an agency that needs to see the numbers but shouldn't change anything.

Common problems

- No data after a week: check that the dates cover a long enough period, and that you verified the exact URL you're testing. https://example.com and http://example.com are different properties.
- Clicks drop to zero overnight: check the date range. A short range can look like a collapse. It can also mean a page was removed, or that its title and meta description stopped matching what people search for.
- "Not indexed" after a redesign: a new template may have added a noindex tag to every page. Search for "noindex" in the new code, or ask whoever did the redesign.

What GSC doesn't tell you

It shows what happened in Search. It doesn't show sales, leads or time on page, and it can't tell you why someone clicked. For that, connect it to Google Analytics, or use your own analytics tool, and compare its numbers with GSC's. If the two disagree, trust the tool you set up first, and check that both count the same period in the same way.

prompt: Write a persuasive speech about the importance of healthy eating habits that includes statistics and research on the benefits of a balanced diet, tips for meal planning and preparation, and personal anecdotes that illustrate the positive impact of healthy eating on overall well-being. Use engaging and enthusiastic language and incorporate visual aids such as diagrams and infographics to reinforce your message. Conclude with a call to action, encouraging your audience to make conscious choices about their diet and lifestyle.
completion:
Look at the plate in front of you. It is the most important decision you will make today, and the next one after that.

I want to persuade you that healthy eating is not a restriction. It is how you take care of yourself.

Start with what we know. In 2017, the Lancet published a massive study of nearly 195 countries. It found that poor diet was responsible for about 11 million deaths a year, more than any other cause except high blood pressure. Most of those deaths came from too little whole food: too little fibre, too little fruit and vegetables, too little whole grain.

Look at the diagram on the screen. It is a pie chart of those deaths, and the slices are labelled with the foods that were missing. It is a sobering picture. But look at the next slide. It shows what happens when people eat more of those foods. The research is consistent. Diets rich in vegetables, fruit, legumes and whole grains are linked with lower rates of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, certain cancers and dementia. One large review in the JAMA Network Open in 2021 found that people who ate the most ultra-processed foods had a much higher risk of dying from any cause than those who ate the least.

Now let me tell you why I believe this, from my own life. I was raised on convenience food. My mother worked long shifts, and the freezer held the family. By my mid-twenties I was tired every afternoon, my blood pressure was high, and my doctor told me to lose weight or start medication. I changed what I ate, more slowly than I wanted. By the third month I was off the medication. The energy came back first. Then the mood. My doctor called it the best blood work she had seen all year.

I will not pretend it was easy. The first few weeks were hard, and I ate badly some days. What worked was small and repeatable: one vegetable at every meal, water instead of soda, and dinner at a table.

So how do you start? Begin with one meal. Breakfast is the easiest place to start. Add one source of protein, like eggs or yoghurt or beans, and one piece of fruit. Then look at your next six days. What is in your kitchen?

This is where planning matters. On Sunday, spend one hour. Pick three or four lunches you can make ahead, such as a grain bowl, a soup or a large salad. Cook twice when you can, so that Thursday's dinner becomes Friday's lunch. Keep it simple. A stir-fry, a lentil curry and a roast chicken all leave something over. Buy frozen vegetables if fresh ones go bad in your fridge. They are just as nutritious, and you will use them. And eat slowly. Your brain needs about twenty minutes to catch up with your plate.

Here is the slide I want you to remember. It is a simple diagram: eat mostly plants, cook at home when you can, keep water nearby, move your body, sleep well. Each one stands on its own. Together they multiply.

Now I want you to picture this. Imagine every person in this room makes one honest change this week. Maybe it is the breakfast you have every morning. Maybe it is one home-cooked dinner a day. Across a city, across a country, those changes add up to something huge. Most of the preventable sickness in the world is tied to what we eat. A population that eats well is a population that falls sick less, loses less time at work, and spends less on treatment. That is a better world, and it is in your hands.

Here is my challenge to you. By Friday, write down three things you will eat this week, and tell one person about them. Say it aloud. The evidence is strong. The habit is yours to build.

Thank you.
